speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to our powder puff negotiator, the Minister of State for International Trade. The minister has just returned from a trip to Japan, where he has failed in his negotiations in every way, shape and form on behalf of the Canadian auto industry. He has come back without one encouraging word for the industry which, as he knows, is suffering from record high unemployment and bankruptcy in the parts sector. All the minister had to say about his failure on that matter, before he returned, was that "he was not concerned." Therefore I would like to ask the minister if he could at least tell this House and, more important, the industry, just what he considers to be acceptable target objectives in this very important matter, before even more jobs are lost.

That this House condemns the government for
a)	proceeding to abandon the Crowsnest Pass freight rate;
b)	failing to implement the recommendations of the Hall Royal Commission;
and
c)	failing to nationalize CP Limited and build a modern, integrated transportation system to create jobs, develop the economy, and enhance national unity.
He said: Madam Speaker, throughout the entire history of our country, the people of Canada have carried on an exercise in co-operative federalism in sharing the costs of running our economy, and particularly transportation, in all regions of the country. One can start in the Atlantic provinces, where we shared-with the people there-the costs of moving the agricultural, processed and manufactured goods within the Atlantic provinces to central Canada. We willingly agreed to tariffs to protect the manufacturing industries in central Canada, and those costs have been shared by all Canadians. We agreed to share in the costs of construction of massive infrastructure for the aircraft industry and the St. Lawrence Seaway. We also agreed to share in the costs of transporting

March 25, 1982
Supply
some agricultural production out of western Canada to export position. I call it co-operative federalism. In our terms, it is a foundation of a co-operative commonwealth.
A number of myths have been perpetrated and emphasized by those who would like to do away with the Crowsnest Pass or statutory grain rates. I would like to spend a few minutes in dissolving those myths. The first one is that the railways lose money hauling grain. They have never lost money hauling grain. They have received full payment, both directly and indirectly, since the first railway was built.
1 want to illustrate by using the figures for the year 1980 in which, at most, the railways lost $10 million hauling grain. If one uses the formula devised by Mr. Snavely in his third report, under the terms of reference ordered by the minister, the railways' costs for hauling grain for 1980 amounted to $671 million. That included a 25 per cent return on investment; it included $123 million of add-on profit; the revenues received by the railroads using the Snavely commission, Transport Canada estimates and publics accounts, amounted to $538 million. Mr. Speaker, they got $132 million from the grain producers; they got $193 million from branch line subsidies; they got $70 million from branch line rehabilitation; they got $4 million in boxcar repairs; and $9 million in hopper car lease; and $116 million saved them in interest charges on the hopper cars purchased by the various governments from the Canadian Wheat Board. Mr. Speaker, they have been fully compensated. That is the case in almost every year you want to look at. Certainly it is the case in every year that I have looked at.
The minister complains that the grain producers pay only 20 per cent of the cost of hauling grain. Why is he picking just on the grain producers? Using the same Snavely formula, cost recovery on hauling grain would be 46 per cent. On the St. Lawrence Seaway cost recovery is only 20 per cent, using the Snavely formula. On the National Harbours Board the cost recovery is 43 per cent, using the Snavely formula. On our highways and roads system, using the Snavely formula, cost recovery is 32 per cent. For Mirabel airport, the cost recovery is 14 per cent; and for Pickering it is only 2 per cent.
Why the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) chooses to pick on the grain producers, when everyone else gets subsidies as large or larger, is beyond me. It has been said that the Crow rate is an unfair transportation subsidy. Well, of the $2.4 billion in transportation subsidies, $277 million went to grain movement; $971 million went for air subsidies; $335 million for marine; and over $500 million for VIA Rail.
Wrong figures for air.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the minister picks on the grain producers. May I also remind the House that one of the main items of logic towards keeping the Crowsnest grain rate for grain producers is that it allows the grain producer to compete in the international market. The United States grain producers have access to massive inland water
systems, entirely built, paid for and operated by the public of that country. That allows them the cheapest form of transportation for most of the grain near the Missouri, Ohio and Mississippi River systems and in some of their canal systems. It allows them to put the grain into export position at a lower cost.
The Argentine raises almost all its grain within 300 or 400 miles of salt water and for the longer distances of their grain haul the Argentine government pays all of the transportation costs. Australia produces most of its grain within 200 or 300 miles of export position. Since this country as a whole, all of Canada, benefits to the tune of four billion or five billion a year in a foreign exchange benefit, surely it is only fair that the nation as a whole share in the cost of getting that grain to export position, just as we share in the cost of transporting goods out of Atlantic Canada or in Atlantic Canada, just as we share in the cost of building airports, seaways and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, this is myth No. 2: grain is a main roadblock to increased western grain capacity. Everyone agrees that rail capacity in western Canada has to be increased and will require a massive investment of many billions of dollars. To lay the blame for that lack of capacity on grain producers is both unfair and unreasonable. Mr. Speaker, "It ain't wheat, it's coal". The department's own figures show that by 1986 or 1987 only about 14 per cent of that capacity will be required for grain; the rest will be for coal, potash, sulphur and other products like that.
Canadian Pacific coal.

Mr. Speaker, I have a strange feeling, a suspicion, that there are some companies and bureaucrats slobbering outside the door of the Minister of Transport, waiting to get some action going on the coal blocks held by the Government of Canada. Canadian Pacific was required to cede 50,000 acres to the federal government by 1904. Several federal departments and the government of British Columbia have been bickering about it. The reserve on those lands was 7.8 billion tons, and if you multiply that by $60 to $100 a ton, you have enough revenue to goldplate the rails all the way to the Pacific Coast. The government holds rights under the Crowsnest Pass Agreement Act for 50,000 acres of coalbearing land in southern British Columbia. The development of those coal blocks is not possible without revocation of the Crowsnest Pass Agreement Act, the legislation which limits prices for the sale of this coal to $2 per ton. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that is why the minister and his cohorts say that Crow must go-"It ain't just wheat, it's coal."
Mr. Speaker, myth No. 3; raising grain freight rates will result in increased livestock production and processing in western Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, does anyone really believe, is anyone under the delusion, that the massive livestock and dairy industry in Ontario, in southern British Columbia, the hog arid dairy and livestock industry in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, are going to hold still for something like a $20-a-ton increase in their cost for feed grain? I doubt very much that Quebec or Ontario would hold still for that. I am
March 25, 1982

pretty certain that the federal government will be the first in line to pay some subsidies to recover the increased cost of feed grains for the benefit of those feeders, livestock producers and dairy producers in eastern Cana- i and in British Columbia.
Give the westerners a chance,

It is a delusion suffered by the cattlemen, by what I call the Texas cowboy syndrome, that they have been suffering in southern Alberta and Saskatchewan for many years. If they were so right, I cannot understand why most of the packing industry pulled out of western Canada; if they had such a good advantage, why didn't they stay?
The statutory grain rates are so fundamental to our history, our economy, the strengthening of confederation and national unity that even the slightest consideration to requiring grain producers in western Canada to pay more can be called nothing less than a betrayal and traitorous. Those who want to destroy the statutory grain rates for our grain producers are the ones who started the row in the first place. It was not the grain producers who raised the issue. I think the first occasion it was raised was in Winnipeg in the mid-seventies by a former minister of transport.
With them are the railroads naturally, although I do not think they particularly care where the money comes from as long as they get it. Who else supported the destruction of the statutory grain rates for western grain producers? This minister and his two predecessors wanted them changed. Naturally the cattlemen's association, the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange, some of the specialty crop raisers whose grain does not come under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board-
What about the Government of Alberta?

The minister raises the Government of Alberta. I am glad he did. We will be able to use that in the coming weeks. We can also use some quotes from Conservative Members of Parliament, but I will not belabour the House with that today. There are two provincial governments, the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, the cow-calf operators of western Canada, the National Farmers' Union and, no question about it, the majority of the membership of the Saskatchewan wheat pool want the Crowsnest rates kept for our grain producers.
Why the government would even consider flying in the face of what was said by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall is beyond me. It is the most definitive study ever done on the principle of statutory rates, particularly those that apply to grain. I remind the House that if the statutory rates for grain can be tampered with and increased, it will automatically lead to raising, if not cancelling, the maritime freight rate subsidies.
If our prairie grain producers have to pay by 1987 what Mr. Snavely calls for, 5.1 times the Crow, that means a cut in net farm income of 36 per cent. Farmers will have less income to spend on the purchase of trucks, tractors, fertilizer, sprays and other supplies. It could mean the loss of another 51,000 jobs
Supply
for Canadians, many of them in the industrial heartland of this country.
The government should make these investments in increased western rail line capacity, but in return for those investments it should obtain equity. How much more do we have to give the railroads in order for them to carry out or have the capability of carrying out their responsibilities? Canadian National has had over $2 billion of its bonded indebtedness taken off its books and transferred to the books of Canada, making the people of Canada the only shareholders in that corporation. As a result, Canadian National has been relieved of paying anywhere from $30 million to $100 million a year in interest charges on that debt. Our shares in Canadian National are an investment which have returned great benefits to this country.
Canadian Pacific is a similar case. It is not only just the millions of acres of land given to them along with the mineral rights from 1881 on, it is also the cash they were given. As a result of those benefits, the investments they made to develop subsidiary companies have returned to them billions of dollars. This has more than compensated for any alleged loss in moving western grain.
Since 1881 we have provided Canadian Pacific with billions of dollars in annual subsidies. In fact, during most of the decade of the sixties, had it not been for federal government subsidies, Canadian Pacific would have shown net losses. This was at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada.
We in this party say that if you are going to provide capital and put it into either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, it is not unreasonable to get equity in return for that investment. I agree it would only be a paper entry in terms of any funds given to Canadian National. It would just increase the shares we own. In the case of Canadian Pacific, it is money the minister suggests will have to be spent over the next four or five years. If we obtained equity in return for that capital, the people of Canada would own 20 per cent of the shares of Canadian Pacific Limited, which means control of Canadian Pacific.
I do not know of any private enterpriser who would agree to put capital into a company without getting equity in return. I have never heard of such a thing, but that has been perpetuated by successive national governments since 1881. To compound the felony, when you look at Snavely's third report, he not only wants them guaranteed a 25 per cent return on investment plus another 22'/2 per cent add-on profit, but he includes in that investment the CPR mainline track from Port Moody to Kamloops, which was built entirely by the taxpayers of Canada, to be turned over to Canadian Pacific at no cost. Mr. Snavely says that Canadian Pacific should get a 25 per cent return on that investment. That is not equitable, it is robbery.
I do not understand why the minister would resist taking equity in Canadian Pacific Limited. There has certainly never been any objection to taking equity in other corporations in this country. Having equity gives you some say as well as control in the operation of that system. In conclusion, I remind

March 25, 1982
Supply
the House that this issue is so basic to confederation that anyone who tries to tamper with it does so at their peril.
We also welcome what I believe to be the unanimous support of the members of the official opposition, albeit reluctantly by some who had to be dragged, kicking and screaming, into it. We welcome the support of the Saskatchewan Progressive Conservatives, albeit reluctantly on the part of their leader, who said that two thirds of the grain producing farmers must go. Of course, we welcome the support of the Saskatchewan Liberal Party, which is led by a former member of this House. I hope that the minister will add that name to the list of those who want to keep the Crowsnest Pass rate for the producers.
If it is proven through whatever formula is chosen that the railways are losing money hauling grain, we would not object to the railroads being paid the difference between the compensatory rate and the Crow rate. We would insist that it go directly to the railroads and that the money must be invested in the railway plants. The rates would continue on the basis of maintaining the statutory rates for the grain producers, equal rates for equal distance and no variable rates. We also say that if there are any proven losses, that is a separate matter. If the government and the Parliament of Canada decides that those proven losses should be made up to the railroads, then let us do so by all means.
It is not necessary to change the statutory grain rates. It is only a matter of making a decision in the public interest to make up that difference directly to the railroads as is done in so many other areas. If user-pay was applied, no one could afford to fly, drive a car, ride the bus or put a boat in the Seaway. If you are to have full cost recovery, it would be necessary to double and triple current air fares as well as raise the marine rates so high that no shipping concerns would wish to enter our ports, let alone the Seaway.
To return to my opening remarks, this is how we share the costs of our nationhood. Surely that is fair and civilized and demonstrates how we can treat one another decently and civilly. It shows how we can keep a united country. It is not just a question of whether the farmer is paying 18 cents or 20 cents a bushel to ship his grain; it is whether or not Canadians are paying for the cost of keeping the nation united through co-operation, trust and fairness.
I believe that the single issue of statutory grain rates has much greater ramifications. The consequences not only concern grain producers in the three prairie provinces; it means much more to the whole country. I hope that the minister will decide to keep the statutory grain rates in place and that any additional funds required, for the two railways in particular, for capital investment in western transportation in return for equity and any operating subsidy required will be continued, but that money given to the railways for branch lines, branch line rehabilitation and interest charges saved on hopper cars and other equipment will be counted in those subsidies. Only then can additional moneys be expended for the full recovery of operating costs.
I do not know what else I can say in order to persuade the minister and the government that this is the wrong course of action and will cause irreparable damage to our nation, particularly western Canada. Although this issue may not be significant enough to contribute to the destruction of Canada, it merits the necessity for Canadians to work together again in sharing the cost of what is a fundamental necessity for Canada.
I hope members who speak after me during this debate will delve into other aspects of the argument. I also hope that members opposite will study the issue from the different aspects which I have mentioned, namely, the sharing of the cost of running the country and keeping our western grain producers in particular in a competitive position with other producers in the international grain trade. This area is so crucial to our entire economy that I submit it cannot be ignored.
Although we cannot have a vote on this resolution, it is my hope that the House will agree that the motion is valid. With that agreement I think we could go a long way to accomplish much more during this session of Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration);
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who preceded me indicated that this is a debate about a view of the nation. I agree with him on that. There is no question that what we are debating here today are two very different perspectives of where Canada should be heading. On the one hand, we hear a plea from the NDP to keep the status quo. We hear a plea for the past, a plea for retrenchment, a plea for reaction and regression. The NDP want us to hold the line. They do not want us to make any changes or to have any vision. They want to hunker down in their corner and protect the old traditions of the past.
You did not listen, Lloyd.
We are prepared to put forward a vision of the future, one that sees opportunity and progress in the prairies.
Visions of the CPR is not a vision of the future.

I will get to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) very soon because I want to address remarks to his constituents, especially in view of the stand he has taken. We want to have a vision which provides an opportunity for the prairies to divesify. We are talking about a new industrial strategy and vision for western Canada where there will be the opportunity to diversify the economy, redress the grievances of the past and bring about a stability and growth in that economy which will place the western region at the forefront of economic growth in Canada. We are not prepared to buy the argument proposed by the NDP and their counterparts is Saskatchewan.
And Ralph Goodale.

Their argument is based upon fabrication. We saw what trouble they had in question period when they
March 25, 1982

were fumbling with the facts. We know how loose and goosey they are with the facts-anything to get 15 seconds on the evening news. What we have over in the corner opposite is Canada's great fog machine. All they can produce is a great cloud which completely shrouds the truth. They are not capable of understanding the reality of the situation.
I am afraid that the New Democratic Party caucus has been too busy reading the fiction produced by the NDP in Saskatchewan. Mr. MacMurchy, the great ad man, is travelling around the country from town to town and meeting to meeting, taking his shoe off and banging on the desk, claiming all sorts of wild and totally unbelievable claims about the proposal that we made for the Crow rate. The claim is that we are going to get rid of the Crow and that that will cost western farmers 13 times the present cost.
It seems that members of the New Democratic Party are not very good at arithmetic. We have known that for many years, but they seem to have come to a mental block when it comes to dealing with the Crow affair. What we are talking about is a commitment by this government to an additional $600 million per year in perpetuity in terms of the statutory grain rate. I did not hear the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) talk about that. He conveniently forgot that fact, just as Mr. MacMurchy seems to forget about it. We are not talking about doing away with the Crow; we are talking about a major commitment by the federal government to establish a new statutory rate to which we will contribute six hundred million additional dollars per year.
It seems incredible that in a debate which is so serious and important to the growth and development of our region in western Canada and to the prospects of this country, members of the New Democratic Party are not prepared to deal with what is real, what is true and what is fact. They seem to have blocked their vision, and we know why. They have a certain base and constituency, and what we are seeing is the evolution of the NDP into the real reactionaries of the west. They are the people who are incapable of thinking in progressive terms. They are not swimming with the stream of the new generation of westerners who are trying to develop a new basis for enterprise and entrepreneurship in the west, who want to develop industry and new processing plants, create new work for the railroads and develop new centres of research. Members of the New Democratic Party are not interested in that. They are interested in harking back to the brave old days of the 1920s and the Regina manifesto. Those were the halcyon days when they were going to create a magical crusade, the children's crusade of Canada. It is unfortunate because this debate is too important for Canadians to be ground into the prairie dust with that kind of fiction.
The fact is we are debating something which could be one of the most important investments this country could make in its future. We are talking about one of the largest megaprojects.
Supply
We are talking about $13 billion of investment in a brand new and modern transportation system which not only will provide for a substantial increase in capacity to move goods to market but also increase the agricultural output of the west by $2 billion in 1990. It will also provide for a wide variety of new jobs and employment in western Canada.
I sit here with some interest watching members of the New Democratic Party from Manitoba and the city ridings of Winnipeg. They seem to ignore, for example, the study which was put forward by the city council of Winnipeg. That is not a one-sided body. On that council are members of all parties.
The council is run by the ICEC, and you know it.

The Winnipeg city council pointed out that one of the most serious drawbacks to the development of manufacturing in the city of Winnipeg has been the existing Crow rate. The council also talked about the closings of the Swift plants in St. Boniface, Edmonton and Regina being the direct result of existing grain rates.
Oh, oh!

Hon. members say that is not true. I have the study here; I will be glad to table it for hon. members. Perhaps members of the New Democratic Party are not interested in listening to facts or listening to the Winnipeg city council.
We are.

All they want to do is yell. They have very loud voices, and I suppose they enjoy listening to the echoes in the echo chambers between their ears. They are not prepared to accept the facts. I want the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill to go back to his riding and tell his railway workers that he is prepared to give up 2,000 additional jobs for railway workers in Manitoba because of his stand on the Crow rate.
Nothing to do with it.
I want the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow)-
Come up and run against me. You run in Winnipeg-Birds Hill and we will see.
We will be glad to run a good candidate against the hon. member. We want him to tell his railway workers-
Any time you want.
Aren't they getting excited, Mr. Speaker?
Resign and we will have a by-election.

We have obviously plunged the needle into their veins because they certainly are spouting a lot of blood on the floor of the House of Commons. We can always tell when members of the New Democratic Party hurt because they bleat. They are bleating very loud and long this afternoon.

March 25, 1982
Supply
The fact is that what we are talking about is an opportunity to develop major new manufacturing in western Canada, to develop employment for tens of thousands of westerners, and to provide the opportunity to increase substantially and enhance our agricultural products, livestock, grain processing and grain production itself.
We are talking about a vision of the future. We are talking about the willingness of this government to take a stand and to open a debate in western Canada and across Canada on one of the most important items which will lead to the development of the economy of this country and the economy of the west.
Let's have public hearings.

We are very pleased and proud that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has been prepared to take that stand. Lie has received the endorsements of a wide variety of western groups for his stand.
It seems that the members of the New Democratic Party are afraid of dialogue. That is the great party of democracy. In the House hon. members are always asking that we get into debate.
Public hearings.

They are afraid to get into an honest consultation whereby farm groups have the opportunity to sit down and put their points of view on the table and look at what they can produce in our economy. No one is going to cook the books for them. They can come to Dr. Gilson, present their facts and figures and talk about what is really taking place. Out of that will come a report and recommendation which will then be debated in the House of Commons. What could be a clearer, more open process of policy making than that?
But members of the New Democratic Party are afraid of that process, and I know why. They are afraid of what it will show. It will show that the kind of conventional shibboleth on which they have been hanging their hats for years will be proved false and wrong. It will show that they are simply captives of the past and that their stand is not one which will promote the progress in which we in western Canada are interested.
Over the past year the western affairs cabinet committee has spent many months meeting with a wide variety of western groups. That committee met with literally hundreds of westerners who spoke to ministers on the committee. The committee met with these people in private and in the open to discuss the economic future of western Canada. One message came through loud and clear, and that is that we must modernize the transportation system. We must have a transportation system which can move our grain and our commodities. We must have a system of rates which allows for proper manufacturing and processing in the west. We must have a transportation system which guarantees the future of western Canada.
That is the basis upon which all our history is founded. There was no disagreement about that. There was certainly
disagreement about the different methods which might be used and the different formulae which could be proposed.
It is for that reason that we have recommended-and our cabinet colleagues accepted it-that the next step in that process should be dialogue and consultation to arrive at what the proper formula should be. No one was prepared to take the first step, so one of the major commitments this government made was to put $1.3 billion on the table as our commitment to western Canada and to the modernization of the transportation system. We realized we were not going to move this debate off dead centre, where it had been for years, unless someone was prepared to put hard money on the line and was prepared to make a major investment, a major commitment of large amounts of money to the improvement, expansion and modernization of our transportation system. That is what we did through the western fund. That is the kind of commitment this government has now made, and that has broken the log jam. We are now in a position where the parties are prepared to talk. The result of consultations right across the west is that people are prepared to come to the table to present their cases and offer their different formulae.
The NFU and the NDP, those two brothers of blindness, are not prepared to enter into that kind of debate and discussion.
What about Ralph Goodale?
What about the Liberals in Saskatchewan?

The NFU and the NDP are not prepared to enter into that discussion. By the very fact that they are entering into that consultation westerners are showing that they are interested in the future and that they are not listening to the siren calls of the NDP federal caucus, which is simply out of step, out of tune and out of time.
The whole point of this debate is to talk about a different kind of future. It is important that we clear up much of the mythology the NDP is trying to conjure up with respect to this matter. Mr. MacMurchy is running around Saskatchewan, as are his colleagues in his caucus, saying that the federal government is going to introduce variable rates, and everyone gets all excited about that. The Minister of Transport and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have said very clearly in Saskatchewan that if westerners do not want variable rates, they will not have them. It is up to them to go to Dr. Gilson and present their case for or against this. If it is the decision of westerners not to have variable rates, they do not have to have them.
We hear the NDP claim that this will ruin rural life in western Canada, that it will have the effect of a wrecking crew in small towns. The authority cited by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) was Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, who pointed out in his study that the primary reason that small towns are being ruined in western Canada is because of the actions of the provincial governments-the new road systems, electrification and all the other programs such as the centralization of the school system. If one examines the reasons for
March 25, 1982

change in the small towns and rural life in the west, it will be seen that they have little to do with changing the Crow rate. The provincial governments are responsible because they brought about the changes. That is the basis of Judge Emmett Hall's report, and he is the man who is quoted as the great authority on railway rates. He should be an equal authority on the impact of those rates on the small towns and rural life of western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, would the minister accept a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the minister want to accept a question?

Mr. Speaker, I will be very glad to accept a question if I have time at the end of my presentation. I could ask the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill how he can justify to his constituents the loss of several thousands-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The minister has the floor.

There are a lot of important questions, and for answers to some of them we must look to those ostriches of the past who dug their heads in the prairie gumbo, unwilling and uncaring about the future. Talk about gophers and groundhogs, Mr. Speaker! Members of that party opposite have not seen the light of day for years.
What we are talking about is the necessity to deal with this question in western Canada on the basis of facts and realism. We are not talking about getting rid of variable rates. We are not talking about ruining small town life either. What we are talking about is the kind of investment that the producers of western Canada have been requesting for years. We are talking about the kind of investment that will restore the urban centres of western Canada to their pre-eminence as transportation centres. We are talking about the creation of employment across Canada, from the steel mills in Sydney to the locomotive shops in Quebec and Ontario and the major urban centres of western Canada. The change in the Crow rate will have multiple benefits for every community across Canada. It will create employment.
The NDP hawk their wares daily. They say, "Create more employment, create more jobs and invest in the country". What we are doing is changing the Crow rate to provide for one of the most important and critical investments that will create employment for tens of thousands of Canadians. Members of that party cannot be so hypocritical as to argue out of both sides of their mouths at the same time and expect Canadians to believe them. They will be found out after a while. They tell their constituents in Saskatchewan that they defend the Crow, and then they come down here and tell eastern workers that they are trying to create more employment for them. Why do they not go to the workers in Sydney, London, parts of Quebec, Winnipeg and Regina and say that they are trying to create more employment by standing against
Supply
any change in the Crow rate, which would bring about a substantial investment of $13 billion in western Canada in the next few years and thus provide countless man-hours of employment in a variety of industries?
How can they try to get away with such duplicity? Their attitude is beyond belief. It is one of the greatest acts of piracy that we have ever seen in this House. They are trying to conjure up in the minds of westerners the idea that this is something that will deprive them of their birthright. Westerners have been asking for a fully developed, diversified economy as part of their birthright, one that is not based only upon raw materials but one that involves a variety of industrial enterprises and thus will not be subject to the cycles of resource markets but, rather, will provide a stable pattern of employment.
We offer an opportunity to put that in place in western Canada. We offer a system that will have enormous impact upon our export markets. It will not only provide an almost $2 billion increase in the export market for raw grain producers, but will provide a wide variety of new markets for processed materials such as oil seeds. Why are the canola crushers so anxious for this change? Why are the commodity producers so anxious for it? It is because they realize that for years they have been deprived of the opportunity of making their case and establishing a firm investment pattern in all regions of the country.
I return the plea of the hon. member for Regina East. If he is prepared to deal with this issue with a sense of honesty, a sense of realism and a sense of the progress which his party says it believes in, then I would ask him to change his position on the Crow rate. He should be prepared to help westerners enter into consultation, to engage in the kind of co-operative approach and participation that we offer so that we can reach a solution that is fully reflective of all issues. We want the inner few at that table. We want all the farm groups there and all interests to be represented. We would ask the NDP to use their good offices with the Saskatchewan government, with the pools and with the inner few to get them to participate and find the best answers for the west and for our transportation system. Rather than raising the flags of negativism and opposition, let them recognize this as a real opportunity for the west to develop fully its economic position.
We return the plea, Mr. Speaker. We have opened up the debate and dialogue and we are prepared to make a major investment in western Canada. We are prepared to enter into wide-based consultation with all groups and all kinds of interests. It is up to members of this House from every party to see that this takes place and it is particularly up to western members of the opposition to use their good offices to ensure that the debate is founded on facts, on figures that are real and not fabricated, on premises that are true, not fiction. They have a responsibility and an obligation to their constituents in western Canada to ensure that such negotiation takes place. If they persist in simply trying to distort, twist, hide and cover

March 25, 1982
Supply
the necessity for the modernization of our transportation system, they are doing a serious disservice to all Canadians.
We return the plea to the NDP and ask that they get on the right track and begin thinking of progress in the country. We ask them to help develop a proper, new statutory rate that will benefit producers and westerners alike.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, is there some time left in the minister's allotment and, if so, would he permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the minister accept a question?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister was speaking of the NFU and the NDP being blind brothers together in this struggle to preserve the statutory rate, I wonder why he left out the Liberal Party of Saskatchewan? Given his supposed interest in the facts, why was this particular fact not brought to the attention of the House in his speech?

Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to correct the record for the hon. member. The Liberal Party in Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia endorsed the Crow rate resolution. We met last Friday with the leader of the Liberal Party in Saskatchewan to discuss it and cleared up many of his concerns. He was also buying some of the propaganda put out by Mr. MacMurchy in Saskatchewan about the variable rates.
In western Canada two governments support the change as well as the western Liberal Party. We hope that if the NDP go back and talk to their own brethren in Saskatchewan they will come on board as well.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my time is limited but I want to open my remarks by observing that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) does not know what a service he has done Mr. Goodale and his political pursuits in Saskatchewan. He knows not what he has done! I think he demonstrated one thing during this debate, and that is that while he may have obtained a new pair of glasses, he still cannot see what the issues in western Canada are and he is doing a disservice to western Canadians in promoting this particular policy.
A lot of people are watching this debate today and a lot of people will read about it. They may be a little mystified by some of the antics that have taken place today. There has been a lot of yelling back and forth between the Liberals and the NDP. People may be a little surprised about that because, as the Canadian public knows, the philosophy of the two parties is very similar. They support very much the same issues and on many important issues they stand together, like Tweedledum and Tweedledee.
There is a story which I think is probably true about Noah's ark. The story is similar to the relationship we see between the NDP and the Liberal party. The New Democratic Party supported the Liberal government on 19 different confidence motions. It supported the government through thick and thin on every important issue. We remember when the leader of the New Democratic Party said that the constitutional document is a very civilized one. He stood four-square behind the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on this particular issue. On important economic issues, such as defeating our government on its budget which would have resulted in progress for the country, the NDP and the Liberal party were together. They are together on every issue. By the time I finish my comments today, I hope to demonstrate precisely what is happening with respect to this issue.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would the hon. member permit a question?

Mr. Speaker, I only have 20 minutes. If I have time remaining at the end of my remarks, I would be glad to do so.
In any event, at the time of the flood there were two animals of every species on Noah's ark. Noah was somewhat concerned with respect to the cats. In order to ensure that there was no hanky-panky between the cats, he decided to put two animals to watch. He chose the two giraffes because they had long necks. He said to the giraffes, "Now, you watch to make sure that nothing happens here which might increase the number of passengers, because we have a full load". Well, after 40 days, the platform came down and off came the animals two-by-two, except for the kittens. There were 19 of them following the two cats. Noah said to one of the giraffes, "I thought I put you in charge of this; you were supposed to watch what was happening". He said, "I am sorry, Noah, I thought they were just fighting"!
That is exactly what we have on the floor of the House of Commons-the NDP and the Liberal Party pretend to fight, but they are together on so many issues.
Canadians will understand, particularly with respect to this item, that statements have been made by spokesmen on behalf of the New Democratic Party which indicate that it was prepared to negotiate an end to statutory Crow rate. On the basis of statements made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration, we now know that the Crow rate will be axed. It is not worthy of being axed, but it will be axed to the detriment of western Canadians. If this is allowed to go through, I fear it will be the end of a way of life for our farmers. I submit it will mean the end of the family farm.
In 1977 the Hall commission made two significant and fundamental recommendations. The first was the retention of the Crowsnest statutory rate, and the second was that the
March 25, 1982

difference between the statutory rate and the cost of transporting grain would be paid directly to the railways. To ask western Canadian producers to pay commercial rates for hauling grain is to ignore an historical and statutory right, to ignore the competitive realities of the marketplace and to ignore the natural and artificial advantages of competing countries.
I am glad to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) present in the House because I should like to give him some advice. I ask him to change his advisers who set up the place of meeting to discuss the Crow rate in Saskatchewan. He went to the town of Delisle which is a great town in my constituency. Whoever was the Liberal adviser who told the minister to go to Delisle, Saskatchewan, should receive the golden finger award. The minister was sent to the hotbed of people who were very much opposed to his position. Last fall I attended a barbecue with 1,000 other people. The minister went there to meet with 1,000 farmers and he was barbecued.
I was on ice!

That is right, the minister was put on ice. I am very serious about this issue. I am sorry that the western representative in cabinet has taken such a position on this very important issue. As I say, Canadian grain producers must meet the competition of the international marketplace. They purchase their inputs in a Canadian marketplace which is protected to some extent. Any increase in freight costs will result in an automatic reduction of their earnings. Any reduction will impact upon the industry as a whole and particularly upon those who are dependent upon it.
On a more basic level, this situation for westerners, particularly those in my province of Saskatchewan, is very much like the situation in respect of the language rights of residents of the province of Quebec. It was part of the confederation package between Canada and the prairie provinces; it is the prairie Magna Carta. I ask hon. members from all parts of Canada to remember this in the months and weeks to come. We came to the bargaining table with different needs and aspirations. We have a collective duty to protect the rights won by the respective partners to this great pact. This plan sounds the death knell for untold numbers of rural communities and, in general, for the rural way of life.
Many hon. members in the House will not understand the social and cultural fabric of the west and how important it is to westerners. Many will not understand how vulnerable it is to destruction from economic forces at work at this time. Western Canadian producers cannot afford any increase in the Crow rate. Next year farm income will drop by 15 per cent. Farm costs will rise by 25 per cent in 1982, after a 63 per cent increase over the last two years and 89 per cent over just one three-year period. Where does that massive increase go? Well, 55 per cent to 60 per cent of that money goes into the hands of the federal government. Massive amounts of money, possibly $51 billion, will flow out of the west in the next five years. Aside from those figures, the cost of maintaining the Crow to the federal government is paltry.
Supply
I am appalled at the lack of respect the federal government has shown the producers of western Canada in moving to change the Crow when there is substantial and fundamental opposition. I cannot understand the Prime Minister coming to the city of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and saying that the people protesting against a change in the Crow rate are uninformed. I represent those supposedly uninformed people and I will take their attitude over that of the Prime Minister any time. What did he say when he arrived in Saskatoon? He was asked a question about the statutory rate. In his response he said that the government cannot please all the people all the time, everywhere on everything. He said that he had yet to go to an open rally in a province where someone has not said, "Why should we pay the shot?" Here it happens to be prairie farmers and "big deal", says the Prime Minister. What kind of attitude is this for the Prime Minister of the country with respect to the legitimately held views of a very significant and important part of our population, the western grain producers? It is no wonder that every time the Prime Minister goes to western Canada he increases the votes of hon. members of the opposition by 2,000 to 3,000. It is because of his attitude, his arrogance and his insensitivity to western problems.
The people of western Canada see this situation as a lack of faith in western Canada. The Minister of Transport indicated that a decision will be imposed if no consensus is reached out of the Gilson hearings. I say to the minister who is sitting here now that this is unacceptable. The people of western Canada understand the game. They feel that the Liberal government says, "What do we have to lose in western Canada-nothing political". The government has shown, its concern for the farming community in its budget; it can just as easily give the west a shaft over the Crow rate. There is nothing in the budget and it is getting even worse treatment in terms of this particular issue.
I have warned before, and it has now come to pass, that the so-called western development fund will be the vehicle by which Liberals will make up the Crow gap in 1982. This fund, the $4 billion elusive dream of the October 28, 1980, budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), is now the $1.3 billion nightmare for westerners. Is it any wonder westerners have so little faith in the Liberal party and its policies? First of all, the federal government announced in 1980 a $4 billion fund to promote the modernization of the grain handling and transportation sector, as well as to promote western industrial diversification. Then in the 1981 budget the government slashed it by 60 per cent. In February, 1982, the federal government used that money as a handout to the railways without tangible guarantees as to how it is to be used. If the government can slash that fund once, they can slash it again. I thought The Globe and Mail in a recent editorial stated the case very well when it said this:
The fact is that the prairies do not trust the federal government. They have no faith in any promises Mr. Pepin may make, no faith in any promises the government may make. They have the Crow. They will stick to the Crow.

March 25, 1982
Supply
Will the federal government ever, Mr. Speaker, grasp the idea that it takes action, not promises, to win back a totally disillusioned electorate?
My specific concerns about the proposal are innumerable, but I want to outline a few. First of all, the entire process is taking place outside of Parliament. Once again it is not Parliament that will examine a major change proposed by the government. It has apparently forgotten that Parliament exists. The whole process is to take place behind closed doors. It is remarkable that discussions on a proposed change which can be so devastating in impact will not be open to scrutiny, particularly by the producers affected. The proposal places a ceiling on further government contributions beyond the 198182 shortfall at a time when massive funds are about to flow into federal tax coffers. The proposal opens the door to variable rates, which is absolutely and profoundly unacceptable. Western farmers have not fought for 80 years to maintain the statutory rate only to see it tossed to the wind.
Even if we have a statutory rate as part of the package, the proposed open-ended escalator to be paid for by the producer spells variable rates, and that is wrong. One harks back to the words of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall who gallantly fought against the Crow rate desecration. I quote him:
If once tampering with the statutory rate is accepted or condoned as an item on the bargaining table, all will be lost.
Mr. Justice Hall is a distinguished constituent of mine and I subscribe to his position absolutely. Once the subject is on the bargaining table, Mr. Speaker, it will only be a matter of time until it is lost. There is no position to take except to adhere through thick and thin. The Crow is not bargainable. That is also a statement by Mr. Justice Hall, a perceptive man who has given leadership on so many issues of importance to this country.
After the rates go up, Mr. Speaker, and when the smaller farms and towns start to die, how will the service be any better? There is nothing in this proposal to guarantee that service. Those guarantees must be there before we even think about giving more money to the railways from whatever source. We also want to know how the proposed subsidy will be distributed. The government has given absolutely no indication of that. They have told Dr. Gilson basically this: "We want to dump the Crow. We want to hit all those westerners who dare to refuse to vote Liberal. We do not care what impact it has in the west; you figure out the fine print and do it quickly and quietly."
Why would we do that?

The minister knows that is what the Liberal government is saying to Dr. Gilson. We from western Canada do not accept that way of dealing. We do not stand for the status quo either. We recognize the problems in the present system of moving grain. Under the present branch line subsidy system it is well known that the railways are subsidized to be inefficient, as they clearly have been in many areas. The railways should receive adequate compensation for hauling grain, but the existing statutory freight rates should remain.
We have said the shortfalls should be met by the federal treasury, and adequate guarantees must be provided to ensure adequate capacity and performance. As well, the anomalies in freight rates between processed and unprocessed products must be resolved in some fashion.
Above and beyond the yearly payment of the 1981-82 shortfall, the federal government has an ongoing responsibility. However, the railways must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the producers that they can deliver grain on time in a reliable and effective fashion before additional payments should be made. With deference I say to the minister who has responded on behalf of the government that he has the thing all wrong. You do not go to the farmers and say: "Now, you pay for some-
You are talking about billions of dollars.

-imprecise commitments to improve service and we will see that things happen to the benefit of farmers down the line." He should be saying to the railways: "Get the system in order and then we will come back to the farmers and see whether there is any room to talk at that time." The problem with the minister is that he has it reversed.
The fact, Mr. Speaker, that this proposal is going forward without the fullest consultation really dismays me.
Lots of people know more than you do about it.

1 can hardly believe there has not been consultation, not only with the agricultural organizations and associations but with the producers themselves. We know that in Saskatchewan there is serious questioning, not only in the pools but in all organizations, with respect to the position being taken and the whole process which is going on.
I would like to close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I am interested to see that the NDP has finally brought this motion forward. I would not want to suggest they were more interested in its political effect than in the issue itself. I would be the last to accuse them of any sort of devious frame of mind such as that. However, it is rather interesting that this matter has been on the Order Paper and we were obliged to bring it forward immediately following the announcement while they have let the matter lie until this week. Has it anything to do with the calling of the provincial election in Saskatchewan? I ask that question rhetorically because I know the NDP, all of whom have to take a course in sanctimony before they come into this House, will answer that one-
Before they run as candidates.

That is it, before they run as candidates, says my colleague, the spokesman on a leadership review of the Liberal Party. Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that when they take such a position I wish they would get together with Premier Blakeney, because he has been equivocating. I am sorry to say that, notwithstanding all the material I get in my home, the letters and so on telling me what they are going to stand for. Premier Blakeney has been quoted as recently as
March 25, 1982

January of this year as saying that he was quite prepared to negotiate a change in the Crow rate. In an interview on the CBC he acknowledged that fact. This is the same Premier Blakeney who is going to the people of Saskatchewan, arm in arm, I take it, with-

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, since the House opened last October the Tories have voted with the Liberals 26 times, whereas the NDP did so only 13 times.
Very shoddy business.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is my first debate as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport. It is perhaps very appropriate that I take part in this debate on Crow rate change. I was a little disappointed that the original mover, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), withdrew his support and had his colleague, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), move the motion. I do not know why, whether he was afraid to defend his own motion-
He is campaigning in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -because I come from that part of Saskatchewan. I was born and raised in his riding. I was born and raised in the riding of Humboldt-Lake Centre, where that hon. member, the original mover of this motion, comes from. I am sure that this motion does not represent the wishes of the farmers in his riding. As a matter of fact, my family left Saskatchewan 30 years ago because of the CCF government at that time under Tommy Douglas. My father, along with four sons and two daughters, saw no future in that province because of the lack of foresight of the government at that time. Unfortunately, it is the same lack of foresight of the federal New Democratic Party which will force many farmers out of that province again.
You like the Tories in Ontario?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am sad that I must say that that is a fact and the truth.
What about interest rates?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I can understand the concern of the farmers for the Crow, as it gave an element of security in a changing world for 85 years. However, change must come. It is happening everywhere. Even the Saskatchewan Power Corporation, owned by the provincial NDP government, increased its electricity rates by 8 per cent in 1980 and by 12 per cent in 1981. The provincial government says that it is okay to increase electricity rates, but that it is not okay to increase shipping and grain rates. I do not know how Premier Blakeney explains this double standard that he is practising within his own province.
Supply
I want to show that the changes to the Crow proposed by the government are for the better, not for the worse. The attitude of the NDP, federally and provincially, of opposing any change whatsoever is simply irresponsible. Provincially, it might be excusable because of the Saskatchewan pre-election fever obviously getting in the way of rational debate. It is surprising, however, as in the past Premier Blakeney has taken a much more realistic position.
I would like to quote what Premier Blakeney said when he appeared on a CBC show on May 20, 1977. I would like my colleagues from the NDP and the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to listen very carefully to what Premier Blakeney said at that time. He said:
Now 1 don't want to be quoted as saying that I'm happy to see Crow increase, that's not so, but I'm realistic enough to know that time goes on and costs go on and I think farmers are realistic enough to say that at some time they would look at increasing Crow, provided they receive the same legislated statutory protection they now have for the Crow rate.
There are three aspects to Premier Blakeney's statement. First, as time goes on costs will increase. That is a fact. Second, farmers are realistic enough to realize that at some time in the future they would look at an increased Crow rate. That is a fact. Third, farmers would want legislated statutory proection. That is a fact. That is what the premier stated on May 20, 1977. On February 8, 1982, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) realized Blakeney's forecast of 1977. Why the change of heart in Mr. Blakeney? I do not know why.
Because your family left Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: I do not know why. Even with the imminent election, the scare tactics and misrepresentations are not justifiable. The provincial government produced a beautiful little booklet which I believe is entitled "The Pepin Plan"-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -paid for by the provincial taxpayers and which led the Saskatchewan people astray. They pulled the same tactic with the Constitution and it did not work. It is pulling the same tactic on the Crow rate and it will not work. There have been further misrepresentations. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy)-
That is a misrepresentation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
-referred to the ad man, and he is correct. The Saskatchewan minister of agriculture, Gordon MacMurchy, put out a press release on March 8, 1982, which stated:
Ottawa has only committed itself to a contribution of $612 million for four years-to 1985-no more.
This is totally incorrect. The Government of Canada has committed itself to paying the Crow benefit, estimated at about $600 million, indefinitely, and the commitment will be enshrined in law. This is what Premier Blakeney wanted and still wants, and this is what the farmers want.
Based on an erroneous premise, Mr. MacMurchy went on to calculate alleged losses to farmers in the province of Saskatchewan. However, he completely ignored the concept of sharing

March 25, 1982
Supply
future cost increases to be developed by the federal representatives on Crow. He completely ignored the benefits which could flow from increased grain production and grain prices. He completely ignored the benefits of improved railway performance and a better delivery system. He also completely ignored the potential for savings by producers-
Are you still reading?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
-in reduced on-farm storage costs. I do not think this kind of misrepresentation will get the provincial government anywhere.
Federally, the NDP has clearly missed an opportunity to show some leadership. The major farm groups recognize the need for change. They have agreed to participate in the process and get the best possible deal for farmers. The NDP are saying, "Ho, ho, ho". Well, it is not Christmas time. I will refer them to the list of farmers and farm groups supporting the change in Crow. First of all, there are the prairie farm commodity associations, such as the Western Barley Growers Association with a member membership of 1,000, the Flax Growers Western Canada, the Palliser, the Manitoba and Saskatchewan rapeseed producers, the Alberta rapeseed producers, the Alberta hog producers and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. That is a total membership of over 97,000. The Western Agricultural Conference has lent its support to changing the Crow. Under that group are Unifarm, with 63,000 members; the Alberta Cattle Commission with 13,000 members; the Alberta pool with 55,000 members; the Saskatchewan wheat pool with 70,000 members; the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities with over 2,000 members-
Oh, no, that is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -the United Grain Growers with 60,000; the Saskatchewan milk producers, the Saskatchewan Chicken Marketing Board, the Saskatchewan Turkey Produce Marketing Board and the Saskatchewan Egg Marketing Board. As well, under that group, there is support from the Co-op Hail Association, the Saskatchewan hog producers, the dairy producers co-op and the Manitoba pool. The number of members supporting this amounts to over 300,000. Taking those two groups alone, we have over 400,000 members saying, "Yes, it is time we do discuss a change in the Crow". So much for the "ho, ho, ho" of the NDP. Instead of supporting the farmers they claim to represent, the NDP take the position of the renegade National Farmers Union-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
-an organization which was almost moribund until it found this last vestige of the past to cling to.
Almost everyone recognizes that changes come. I might refer the NDP to some of the editorials which are supporting these changes.
Talk to the people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I refer the NDP to an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press entitled "Unnecessary Issue", which states:
There should be no mistake that those who oppose a change in the Crow are outside the mainstream of western agriculture.
I suggest that the NDP are outside the mainstream of western agriculture. The editorial of March 22, 1982 in the Winnipeg Free Press further states:
In Saskatchewan, it would appear that short-term political advantage is more important.
There is no political advantage for this government to change the Crow rate, as suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon West. However, this government, and I think all hon. members in this House-
There are no Liberals left to defeat. You are right about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -when we are elected, must set goals for the future. We are not building a country-
That's for sure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -for ourselves. We are building a better Canada for generations to come, for our children, our great grandchildren and so on.
Certainly not for today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I wish the NDP would take that responsibility. Its members should just ask themselves what will be the benefits of the change in Crow for future generations.
The NDP is failing to represent the best interests of the farmers. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said in this House, it would be a betrayal not to do anything about the Crow. Members can read in Hansard of February 8, 1982, at page 14748, what the Minister of Agriculture said. He said this:
I think that it would be a betrayal not to do anything about the Crowsnest Pass rate, to accept and go along with the old program, the old agreement of 1897 and not move ahead. If we did all things like that in our country we would not be the envy of the world for our agricultural industry.
1 am proud to be a member of a party that shows it is not afraid to take that stand.
Let us be clear on what the federal government is proposing under this change. First, grain will always have a special status. The process set up by the Minister of Transport will guarantee that this special status will be enshrined in legislation, to give the farmer the security that he or she needs.
Secondly, the government will provide an annual payment- not just for four years-of the Crow benefit, calculated for 1981-82 at some $600 million. This commitment will also be in legislation, as requested by the Premier of Saskatchewan.
The sharing of future costs increases, as suggested by my friend for Regina West, is a matter for negotiation. It is a major part of the Gilson exercise. What could be more democratic than direct negotiations with those affected? This
March 25, 1982

government has always believed in and practised the consultative process. It will always believe in obtaining ideas, suggestions and recommendations from the grassroots of this country. That is what the process will be. There will be requirements of railway performance, service, investments and adjustments in other rates to promote certain agriculture, and a monitoring system to make sure that they do what they are supposed to do.
Also in legislation there will be a mechanism or framework to determine what the rate should be. The railways will not be able to charge what they want-again, as falsely promoted in some of the western provinces.
In the past, the farmer has a guaranteed rate but no guaranteed service. That did not do him or her a lot of good. The Wheat Board said it lost $1 billion in sales in the late 1970s because of transportation problems. The Secretary of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) said recently he knew of six countries which had turned to other markets because Canada could not guarantee delivery through its present rail system. What the government is proposing is that the guaranteed rate be replaced by guaranteed service-I wish to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker-along with a perpetual financial commitment from the government. That is leadership, and I wish the NDP would adopt some of it.
Mr. Speaker, the result will be that the railways will be compensated. Even Premier Blakeney concedes that this is necessary. The farmer will be protected and will have the assurance that he or she will be able to move his or her grain. To me, that is a better deal than the west has had in the past, and I think the NDP should go for it. The governments of British Columbia and Alberta, and the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, are going for this deal, so surely the federal NDP members who were elected to make decisions on what is best for the whole country-not what is best for one region but what is best for the entire country, what is best for future Canadians- will support us in this process to come up with what is an equitable rate for farm producers.
I want to thank the NDP for bringing this topic to the floor of this House on one of the opposition days, because it has given the government an opportunity to set the facts straight, and to correct some of the false statements that the government of the province of Saskatchewan is repeating to its people. They will be able to read what has been said in this House and they will be able to get the truth.
I would like to congratulate the Minister of Transport, not because I am his parliamentary secretary-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: -but because here is a minister who took the bull by the horns, as we used to say out west-
Take the bull by the tail.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
-who has shown leadership, who saw what is best for the future of the country, saw what is best for future agricultural producers. I want to congratulate him in this
Supply
House. He knows what is good for the future of this country and he was not afraid to get up and say so. It is very easy, Mr. Speaker, to refrain from taking any decision, as the NDP continually do. No decision is very easy to take, but it is very tough to take unpopular decisions. Our minister, the Minister of Transport, did take an unpopular decision, but it is a decision that will benefit future Canadians; and that is what we are elected for, to build a country that will be the best in the world.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I find it very interesting that the member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) should say such nice things about his minister. He said his minister took the bull by the horns; he may very well end up with the tail by the time this whole process is through.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: You don't know which end of the bull is which.

Well, I think I raise a few more bulls on my ranch than you do in your little lot in Toronto, when it comes to knowing which end of the bull is which.
I find it passing strange that while farmers are facing some of the worst dilemmas they ever faced since the Depression in regard to costs versus the price they are getting for their grain, we as a national government, under the leadership that the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park is talking about, are discussing making that farmer look forward to paying more for transportation of his grain to the west coast and east coast.
The Minister of Agriculture has been saying some very interesting things. In a speech in Winnipeg he said that between 1975 and 1981 the ratio of farmers' net income to farm cash receipts dropped from 39 per cent to 21 per cent. He went on to say that it might be even worse in the coming year and that the net farm income is expected to drop 15 to 20 per cent in 1982. He was in such a depressed mood at the time, Mr. Speaker, that he went on to say that perhaps he should revise the old Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to try to bring farmers through this period.
The minister responsible for the Wheat Board announced the initial prices yesterday or the day before. The farmers in my constituency are facing a decrease in the initial price that they will receive for grain in 1981-82. For barley it is down 30 cents a bushel; for oats it is down some 31 cents a bushel. All other prices remain the same, no change. Farmers are facing increased costs of production, as was mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We get from the Canadian Wheat Board a lowering of the initial price system. They are not prepared to take their responsibility in the face of this type of income figures. They use the act that they have, the section that is there, where they can borrow money if need be to maintain a price, and they feel that that price is justified and what better time to do that than today as we face these terrible income pictures.
The deputy minister of transport stated, as he was discussing the new proposal on the Crow rate-and this is in the Western

March 25, 1982
Supply
Producer of February, 1982, an article by Mr. Adrian Irwins-that the range of increase looks as though it might be doubled, or maybe tripled, over a period of four or five years. He says that is kind of ballpark. That is the type of statement we get from the deputy minister of transport, Mr. Kroeger, as farmers are looking at the kinds of cost they may face in the future. He says they are not sure whether they will double or triple, and that is why we have the study. Farmers putting in a crop this year do not know whether they will have enough money at the end of the year to pay their costs, let alone enough to live on, yet they are being asked to accept a change in the Crow rate.
No wonder the motion before us today and the motion which the Progressive Conservative Party put before the House on Febuary 26 state that we should be very cautious about the proposals being made by the minister and look for leadership when we are dealing with transportation costs in western Canada. We made a very responsible suggestion. If the railways have been capable of delivering grain for the last 85 years at half a cent a ton mile, perhaps in the next 20 years they will be capable of delivering grain for the $612 million being proposed. If they show that the capacity is there, maybe farmers could then look at whether or not they should pay some increased costs. That is a very responsible suggestion which would take us to the year 2000.
I will be making suggestions which I hope will be looked at. Some excellent suggestions were made by the hon. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall as well as by Mr. Hugh Horner in his study "A review of the red meat industry". Some excellent suggestions could be proposed to help farmers with their income problem. The railways should be given an opportunity to show they mean business in the prairies and are going to take the incentive, the Crow gap, the money being provided by the government, and move the grain.
I want to discuss two suggestions made by people who have studied this area in the last number of years as well as put forward my own suggestion. Hon. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall put forward an excellent suggestion. Another suggestion that should be looked at is in Mr. Hugh Horner's study. The railways have stated this many times. They feel that their branch lines inhibit them. Over the years we have provided subsidies for branch lines. We have never actually seen that money go to grain branch lines; it has always gone into the general operating fund.
There is some difficulty in moving grain across the branch lines. In many cases the hopper cars are too heavy. They cannot be loaded to full capacity. Some $200 million a year go into branch line subsidies, but this is not being used to upgrade them.
In the 1977 Hall report, some suggestions were made that have never been discussed. In chapter V regarding branch lines, four alternatives were outlined. One suggested we should study a mini-train alternative, an independently owned and operated power unit delivering modified grain cars from the elevator to the loading facilities on the main line where the
grain would be transferred to hopper cars. Another alternative was a short line, independently owned and operated loading unit delivering grain from the elevator to the main line train assemblies. He went on to discuss the trucking alternatives. The other was a do-nothing alternative which is a continuation of the present system.
The second proposal, the short line alternative, makes eminently good sense to me. The railroads have never done anything but ask that branch lines be abandoned. Perhaps it is time for us in western Canada to put forward another alternative. The branch lines should be turned over to the provinces as part of the rural rail bed and allowed to be operated by independent owners or co-operatives. That suggestion was made by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall and outlined by Hugh Horner in his study for the Alberta government, his review of the red meat industry. He suggested that grain independent branch lines be transferred to the provinces at a nominal fee and operated by the provinces as part of the rural road system. He discussed the $200 million a year in branch line subsidies and $80 million a year for branch line rehabilitation. These subsidies do not necessarily go to the upkeep of the branch lines. The railways use the money wherever they feel they can get the greatest economic return.
Our motion in February proposed that this issue be directed to the parliamentary committee, for intensive study and the turning over of branch lines to the provinces to be operated as part of their rural rail bed could be part of that study.
These branch lines are analagous to the rural road system. They are an essential part of the infrastructure for rural western Canada and they should not be allowed to deteriorate. The farmers and businessmen of those areas should be allowed to form co-operatives and run them in a fashion that would keep them as an integral part of western rural Canada.
There are many advantages to this system which are outlined in this review. Often when we get excellent reports such as the one by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall and Mr. Hugh Horner they are allowed to gather dust. We go on with what members opposite call leadership, which is just doing away with a program that has been part of western Canada for the past 80 years.
The minister should accept our suggestion of providing the Crow gap, some $600 million, to the railroads and ask for a guarantee of service. In the meantime, we should be allowed to put forward these kinds of suggestions.
If the federal government were to pay that $600 million and set up a task force or royal commission to study the feasibility of turning over the 8,000 miles of branch lines to the prairie provinces at a nominal fee to be run as part of their rural road system, we could establish rural regional rail co-operatives to operate these short-haul lines as part of the rural system of road beds. They could purchase through an incentive plan some smaller locomotives. Huge locomotives would not be required for the operation.
