The grain cars could be transferred to the main line, picked up at regional terminals and pulled to the ports as part of a unit train.
March 25, 1982

The grain could be cleaned at the inland terminals and the screenings used as feed for livestock. We could establish a provincial rail authority to oversee the operation of the system and disperse the revenues and costs to the rural co-operatives. The GTA could still be in charge of rail car allocation. We could very easily put in place the same kinds of tax credits as in the oil industry and movie industry to allow these cooperatives to buy the extra grain cars and locomotives needed to operate the system.
This whole area makes eminent sense to me and is one that should be proposed to western Canada. It is one that the leaders in western Canada should be allowed to discuss so that we do not just have to accept the position being put before western Canada by the Minister of Transport and his one-man committee, who is holding negotiations behind closed doors so that we do not know exactly what is happening.
These ideas, along with those which have been proposed to the Wheat Board during the last few years to assist western farmers, must be considered. Such ideas included an assured market plan which the Wheat Board called MAP. Farmers are now saying that we should take a second look at this program in order to make some changes.
Mr. Jarvis, head of the Wheat Board, has recently been discussing a proposal for a cartel, which is something I have some difficulty with. It is just another name for something that members from all parties in the House have started with the United States, namely bilateral arrangements whereby we would set floor prices so that our two countries, which move approximately 70 per cent of all export grains in the entire world, would not be in such a competitive position that we are actually selling to countries who can afford to pay at below the farmers' cost of production.
If these ideas were being proposed at this time, along with fuel rebates, proper extensions of the small business development bond, plans to assist farmers who face extremely high interest rates and energy expenses during the next five years, then perhaps we could ask western farmers to look at some changes in the Crow rate in the next 20 years.
There is another anomaly which has not been addressed by the Minister of Transport in his Crow rate proposal. It concerns the British Columbia railroad and the farmers who deliver grain from the Peace River region. They have never been included in the Crow rate proposal. The British Columbia government has been paying the Crow difference out of the grain which is coming from the Peace River area for many years now. Until the last couple of years, the Wheat Board had not even been allocating some of the grain cars which were purchased by the government and the Wheat Board to farmers in that area. This situation has been rectified due to the strenuous arguments made by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle).
I believe the Minister should accept this proposal and ensure that the farmers in the Peace River area of British Columbia have their problems placed before the committee which he
Supply
established so that disbursement of moneys may also be made to the British Columbia area. I believe that this is a very important consideration.
I would like to speak for a moment about some of the situations which can happen when an aggressive group is put into a system which, although it has been functioning for 85 years, has not been functioning very well and even deteriorating. When we were the government in 1979 the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who was the Minister of Transport at that time, decided that some emergency plans had to be put in place in order to deliver grain until a system could be worked out to alleviate the many problems in the western grain transportation and gathering system. He convened an emergency grain movement task force of which I was glad to be a part. In a matter of two months we were able to set up the Grain Transportation Authority. We were able to make some 16 recommendations.
Even though nothing changed in the system at that time, the amount of grain which moved from the prairies to the ports increased substantially. To us this indicated that by aggressively addressing the problems in the system it could be made to work at a greater capacity than in the past. This was proven by the task force which was working in the prairies at the time.
We discovered some very interesting things which should have been happening for a long time and were not. We found that we should reduce segregation in the grain terminals and pursue the pooling of oil seeds. The system which had been operating for years was one whereby each grain company demanded that the car which they loaded in the prairies be delivered to their terminal when it came to port, even though the rapeseed was exactly the same in all cars. When a train pulled into Vancouver with some 100 cars, we often had to have 60 to 70 switches in order to get the right cars to the right terminal.
After the task force found that these things were happening, the Grain Transportation Authority went to work and discussed the whole matter. We now find that there is a pooling of oil seed cars, with the result that the turn around in those cars has increased dramatically.
We should employ supplementary quotas to attract grain to our interior cleaning facilities. At a time when there is a shortage of cars and there are cars which go to port with 5 per cent to 15 per cent of weeds in them, just imagine how much more grain we could move if those cars were cleaned in the prairies. There is a need for those screenings to remain in the feed industry of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We can relax some of the cleaning standards for our high grade wheats because they are really not needed.
We can pursue the possibility of making some effort to provide incentives instead of constantly imposing penalties to get our grain moved by the railways and the companies in a more efficient manner. Therefore, there are ways of making the system work more efficiently if Members of Parliament and task forces are allowed to look at new ideas and methods. There is much to be found out.

March 25, 1982
Supply
We are facing some very astonishing statistics concerning the movement of products from the west to our ports.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. 1 regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Speaker, when one is discussing the grain industry in the west, one is discussing a topic which probably gets spoken about more in the House of Commons than any other. I think when one speaks about the grain industry in the west, one is also talking about a subject which has great emotional attachment and we are dealing with a mythology that is very important to a great many people. In debating this subject today we are also debating a subject which is in the very middle of a raging debate in western Canada. We are dealing with something which is alive and well.
I believe we are also debating a subject which I think the House of Commons has very seldom debated. In the eight or nine years since the Hon. Otto Lang first raised the question of the Crow rate, I cannot recall when the subject was debated in the House of Commons so often. One of the reasons some members are unfamiliar with the debate and what has been happening to the railways and to the wheat farmer vis-a-vis the transportation system is that we in the House of Commons have been afraid to touch the subject. This is because we understand the emotional impact that discussion of this subject has back west. We have therefore tended not to deal with this question in the House in an adequate way.
Now that the government has finally made a decision to move and attempt to deal with some of the problems which have been caused by the Crow rate, it is somewhat of a shock and surprise to us all to discover that when we go back to review our own records of our committee hearings there is almost nothing in the file. We are all beginning to learn the facts anew.
In my judgment, having been an advocate of studies of the Crow rate back in the middle 1960s when I came to the House of Commons and joined the Standing Committee on National Transportation, and after spending a year travelling the railways of Canada with the committee which rewrote the National Transportation Act, I can recall what a terrible day it was to those of us who wanted to see the Crow examined when the House turned down the clause in that bill which would have allowed to take place the study as to what the costs and the benefits of the Crow were.
I think that decision of the House in 1967 set us all back in terms of being able to deal with this particular question. Therefore, it becomes much more difficult for us to do it now at a time when the economy is slowing down and at a time when everyone is being forced to tighten their belts.
Why are we doing it now? It is for the same reason that everyone is cutting back in every field. We have discovered that our ambition to spend in the private, corporate and governmental sense is exceeded by the revenue we have to spend. We have now reached the point in the Government of
Canada accounts where 25 per cent of every dollar we collect as revenue goes to pay the national debt. There is just not much money in the bucket any more, and the consequence of that is that the government is examining all its expenditures.
We know when it comes to the railways that there must be massive investments over the next ten years. That money has to come from somewhere, and it is going to come from the Canadian taxpayer, it is going to come from the railways, it is going to come from the consumer of the goods that are moved on the railways, and a greater share will have to be paid by the producer of the goods which move by those railways.
The question we are discussing is: What are the fair shares and what are the amounts each group will pay? I think it is an absurdity to say that the amount paid by the producer of grain is going to disappear. The projections we have-and nobody has challenged them-are that by the year 1990 the grain producer will be paying 2.5 per cent of the cost of moving his grain, yet if we go back 25 years to the middle fifties, we find that the grain producer was paying 75 per cent of the cost of moving his grain. 1 find nothing written anywhere in the statutes of man or in the word of God that says this is the condition that has to go on forever.
Who is paying the cost? Part of the NDP motion today says we should nationalize the CPR.
Right on.

Will that save anybody one cent? My God, when I look at the profits of CP Rail, I see one person who is subsidizing the grain producer, and that is whoever owns shares of CP Rail, because CP is not making any money. The people who subsidize are the railway workers. Every railway worker takes less pay than he would otherwise get because of the subsidy which goes into the system. Everyone who moves freight in and out of western Canada-or almost anywhere in Canada-pays a part of the Crow subsidy, and that subsidy is going up as the amount paid by the grain producer goes down.
The farmer has paid a heavy cost too. We do not have diversification of western Canadian agriculture because of this. One of the things I have taken an interest in is the question of triticale. It is a very interesting subject for those who want to understand the problems the Crow has caused to the agricultural industry. Here we have a new grain. It is probably the only new grain discovered in the last 500 or 600 years. We are not growing very much of it, even thought it was put together at the University of Manitoba. It is grown in Mexico. It is grown in Russia. It is grown in Poland. Only now is it beginning to be grown in western Canada. Why is it not growing in western Canada in substantial amounts? Because it cannot be shipped out of the country, or anywhere, because it has to pay the full rate, and the full rate discriminates against any grain crop produced in western Canada unless it happens to be on the short list which comes under the Crow. What does that
March 25, 1982

mean for farmers in western Canada? It means they are locked into a one-crop economy. That is not very sensible because any economist and any farmer will tell us that what they really want to do is rotate crops and make sure they are able to protect themselves against being wiped out totally by whatever disease or pest might come along.
Let me refer to a story which appeared in the Star-Phoenix of Saskatoon.
A great paper.

"Topsoil drift said fault of Crow rate" is the headline of a story by Nancy Russell on March 18. The story points out that because there is only one crop and not enough variety in what is being planted in western Canada, topsoil is moving on. There has to be a greater range of crops planted, but the Crow works against that. The Crow locks farmers into a very limited number of crops they can grow on an economic basis because they cannot move those crops out. If farmers cannot move them out, it does not make any sense to grow them. If they cannot grow them at a profit, it does not make any sense to grow them.
When we look at the subsidies which are in our system, there are two points we have to remember. The subsidy which goes into the Crow is paid by all Canadians. Who gets the benefit of that subsidy, Canadians or our foreign customers? I put it to hon. members that in point of fact the person who receives the benefit of the subsidies we have built into our system is not a Canadian at all but a foreign customer. This applies not only to grain but also to many other minerals I know we export, and even to some of the manufactured goods we export. I do not mind paying subsidies, but I really would like to see their major benefits reside here in Canada.
The other point 1 want to make about subsidization or any kind of system is that if we do not put into the system the money that is needed to make the system work, it will not work. In the last 25 years we have systematically deprived Canadian railways of the revenue they need to make their systems work. That is why branch lines are down. That is why there has not been the kind of investment the railways should have been making in hopper cars. That is why the Government of Canada and the provincial governments have had to go to the rescue. They have had to buy hopper cars for the railways because the railways are not generating enough profits to be able to buy the cars. This applies not just to cars but to the whole range of things the railways do. We have starved the system, and nationalizing the CPR would not change that one little bit. What has to happen is that more money has to go into the system so that we can bring it up to date. The difficulty is that not having invested enough money in the system in the last 20 years, the investment in the eighties will have to be massive indeed.
The second point about subsidies is that they tend to protect those people who were there first. In the case of the Crow rate, that was the farmer. It is important to recognize that when the Crow rate was developed it did provide enough money to cover the cost. It did provide a little margin of profit. Probably until the end of the Second World War and perhaps into the early fifties there still was not much of a burden, but what has
Supply
happened since then? The basic understanding of governments and the railways about the Crow rate was that instead of costs going down, as had been the assumption, costs went up, and the costs are now escalating at a rate which simply cannot be sustained by the system unless there is a new source of revenue. The question we are debating is where that revenue for capital improvements will come from. Where is that revenue for operating expenses to come from, who is going to pay and how much?
Not the farmers, John.

Why should the farmer be in the position where 25 years ago he was prepared to pay 75 per cent of the cost of moving his grain and in 1990 he insists on paying only 2.5 per cent of that cost? Is there a God-given right to that? Everyone else has to play in the international market. There are very few people who are exempt from playing in the international market, I recall the deals we made in the GATT, and I know the way tariffs are coming down in the next five years. If anyone has any illusions that the old concept of a high tariff country is going to be there for very long, he just has not been paying any attention to what has been going on, and he has not been paying any attention to the inability of our tariff barriers to keep foreigners out. My goodness, the automobile industry is now taking full-page ads in the newspapers of Canada to say that they have no tariff protection. The New Democratic Party has said, "We want 85 per cent tariff protection for the automobile industry". I do not think that is an appropriate way to go, but the NDP has said, "We are no longer a free-trade party from the west; we are now a high-tariff party from Ontario." The New Democratic Party wants 85 per cent Canadian content in any portion of cars coming in. That is crazy, but that is the NDP position. That is certainly what members of the NDP are promoting in the province of Ontario, and that, I take it, is coupled with the NDP position that the manufacturers of Canada should be protected and the farmers should be protected. There is not enough money in Canada to do that.
The dilemma we have in trying to deal with the Crow, in my judgment, is a very simple one. We have a system which has been in place for 85 years. We have a system which, all things being equal, probably would not need to be changed. But all things are not equal. Inflation and increased transportation costs have conspired to put an intolerable burden on the whole railway system. The question we have to ask ourselves is how we can restore the railways so that they will be able to provide us with the kind of service we require to keep our foreign clients on whom the western grain producer is totally dependent.
Nationalization of the CPR would not bring a single additional penny into the system; the money must come from outside. Where will it come from, Mr. Speaker? What are the economic effects of the kind of cross-subsidization that we have? I think there have been two main victims of that form of

March 25, 1982
Supply
cross-subsidization and one has been the west. It has hindered the development of alternative economic opportunities in the west and it has blocked the diversification of agriculture. It means we have been locked into a pattern set in the west in 1896.
Another group of people has had to pay for that subsidy as a result of the total distortion that has taken place in freight rates in Canada, in two ways. The first has been the kind of distortion that in the Canadian rate structure has always put a premium on moving natural resources as opposed to moving manufactured goods. In other words, the way the freight structure was established, largely as a result of the Crow, was that it tended to take resources from the natural resource areas and move them to the cities to be manufactured and then move the manufactured goods back. If we look at the freight rate structure for any natural resource, we will find a bias in favour of the movement of resources to the city. That structure developed as a result of the Crow.
The second bias in the system is that a good portion of the deficit that the railways occur in the movement of grain is covered by the freight shipper on other commodities. That means that potash, iron ore, lumber and all bulk goods pay a higher cost for transportation as a result of the subsidization cost. We in the rural areas pay a higher cost for freight than would be the case if the subsidy did not exist.
While I have a great deal of difficulty with the process developed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in stripping frunds from VIA Rail, I have to say that I think it was a healthy thing to take the cost of subsidization of passenger rail service away from the freight shipper. That was a sound move. I think we should put our subsidies on the table; that is, pay them directly and not try to incorporate them by passing the burden to other people who use the system.
We have to decide where the subsidy is to go. The question is whether it should go to the farmer directly or to the railroad.
I have a strong feeling that, regardless of the administrative difficulties, the subsidy should go to the farmer. I believe that for the simple reason that the farmer takes the risk. He decides what to plant and what market to approach. If the subsidy were paid to the farmer, then he would be in control and could do what he thinks is best.
I recognize that there is an institutional argument for the subsidy to be turned over to the railways, but I do not believe that the railways can necessarily decide what is best for me. I believe that the subsidy should be paid directly to the farmer so that he can make his decisions and, of course, he will make decisions in his best interests. I think my main point is clear, Mr. Speaker. There is the choice of subsidizing an institution, the railways, or putting the subsidy in the hands of the farmers. I believe it would be better not to put it in the hands of the railways but to put it in the hands of the person who can make the best use of it.
I have gone over the minister's proposals in some detail. By and large I have been surprised that this is but a modest step forward. It is not an elimination of the subsidies built into the Crow; basically what we are saying is that the subsidy is going
to be kept at a particular level and that increased costs after that level will be shared in some proportion.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired.

What is the importance of the situation? Agriculture or the production of food in Canada is in a foremost position. As long as it remains number one, Canada will remain strong. We must be very careful not to take steps to undermine agriculture. Wheat is one of the major bases of agriculture, particularly in western Canada, as is the movement of wheat. We in the Progressive Conservative Party stand for upgrading branch lines because there are too many of them which cannot carry hopper cars or are only carrying hopper cars with half loads. This does not make sense. A contribution has been made by the government to upgrading these branch lines and, in many cases, the work is being done. But I could point to rail lines and branch lines in my own area where culverts were moved in and then moved out without any work being done. It is most important to see work done in these areas.
What will the outcome be for farmers? First it will be very dependent upon the attitude of government in the House and the attitude of hon. members regarding this very important issue. We have a commission to study the issue which is conducting hearings at the present time. I should like to say something about this study because there has been a great deal of talk concerning what is really being said by grassroot farmers. I represent grassroot farmers in my riding. I have talked to them and they have said that they want the retention of the statutory Crow rate. It is most important that it be retained.
What about production and its importance to farmers? I should like to indicate a few facts in this regard. In 1905, 90 per cent of all people were engaged in agriculture. They produced enough food to feed the people of North America. Today we have a little over 4 per cent of Canadians who are engaged in agriculture and are producing enough food to feed the people of North America and a good deal of the world. It is important to keep agriculture strong.
What will it do for Canadian consumers? We all know that Canadian consumers purchase the cheapest possible food compared with many other countries of the world. This is an important factor. Perhaps we could argue today that farmers have received an advantage which others have not received. In many cases farmers have purchased under a tariff and have sold on open markets. In many other cases they have purchased in areas where they have paid a third more, and perhaps even 50 per cent more, because of a protected market. 1 remember years when a good truck was selling for $2,000 or $3,000 less in Crosby, North Dakota, than a similar one was selling for in Estevan, Saskatchewan. Why was this? It was because of a protective tariff.
Such things have existed throughout the history of Canada. I am not suggesting that it was wrong in all cases, but I am suggesting today that farmers cannot afford to pay an additional $1 per bushel. I raised this matter with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House on the basis of having personally gone to Alexander, North Dakota, and checked on the price of moving grain from that city to Seattle. The price at that time, which was approximately two years ago, was $1.35 per bushel. Under the statutory Crow rate, wheat is
Supply
moving out of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, at 19 cents per bushel.
I am suggesting to the House that the increased cost in the movement of grain could amount to as much as $1 per bushel in the next four, five or six years. This is a very serious threat to the economy of western grain farmers and of Saskatchewan in particular. This is why I take a strong stand that the statutory Crow rate must remain and that the Government of Canada must make up the Crow gap.
What is our responsibility in this situation? Today we have a very, very irritated western Canada. It is irritated because of the insensitivity of a government which did not understand the western Canadian energy policy. For example, I have spoken with people who are involved in the service and supply industry in Weyburn, Estevan and Swift Current. They indicated that they are only selling 20 per cent of production in southwestern Saskatchewan. On April 1 a new quota will be set for south Saskatchewan which will also restrict production. The people of that area will only be permitted to move 35 per cent of production. They do not understand this severe measure. They do not understand why hundreds of people should be out of work. They do not understand why service and supply companies should be going broke, be forced into bankruptcy and be forced to sell their equipment when Canada needs oil but purchases offshore oil from Mexico at a cost to Canadian taxpayers of $16 per barrel higher, with about $9.06 in incentive grants to refineries, when the same grade of oil is available in Saskatchewan. I want to suggest that people do not understand that. When they do not have jobs you cannot explain why they should have to go through this. If the government and Members of Parliament are as insensitive to the Crow rate as they are on the national energy policy, you are going to have a very serious situation in western Canada. I would like that to go on record here as giving a warning of the existence of a very serious situation, and it is most important that the government and the Minister of Transport be sensitive to it.
I do not feel, Mr. Speaker, that I should belabour the subject. I have made my point. We face a very serious issue, probably the most serious in the history of western Canada. Therefore, I advise Members of Parliament, the government and government backbenchers, to weigh very seriously the issue of the statutory Crow rate and make their decision taking into consideration the future of this nation and the importance of the agricultural industry to this great country of ours, Canada. I thank you.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to be able to speak to this whole issue of the Crow rate. I would like to preface my remarks with a comment about a term we use in sociology, one that I have probably used in one of my first lectures in teaching sociology, namely, ethnocentrism. The idea behind that is that so often we judge other cultures-in this case other regions of Canada-based on our own limited experience, background and academic training. When I think about the fact that the Canada bill has

March 25, 1982
Supply
just been passed in the English House of Lords, and specifically about the clause dealing with multiculturalism, I realize it took a little while for us in Canada to realize that there are ethnic groups in Canada with a different background from those with an English or French heritage. It is of interest to me that reports such as that of the task force on Canadian unity, the Pepin-Robarts report, recognized this diversity. I urge the minister to go back to his own report because it also dealt with the question of regional diversity. There are differences in regions from one coast of Canada to the other. The report asks this question:
What of regionalism, which we have identified as the second line of cleavage in Canadian society which needs attention in the present crisis?
In looking at this report it seems to me we had an intelligent co-author who recognized that there are regional differences.
Indeed.

Looking at some of the specific recommendations on page 125 we see a plea that we:
-recognize the diversity among Canada's regions and the need to permit all regional communities to flourish.
With the knowledge that the current Minister of Transport was involved in that kind of study, I am utterly baffled, dismayed and disappointed that he now fails to recognize the academic rhetoric which is now being used. I think it is important that we look at this whole issue as one which gives us an idea of the nature of Canada; how we are different from region to region, how these historic developments have occurred, and how we can make sure they do not continue to work to the detriment of a specific region of Canada.
I would, therefore, like to focus for a moment on what I might call an historical argument for the retention of the Crow rate, for the importance of painting, as it were, an economic picture of Canada and taking a look at our history. In sociology we would say that as Canada developed, there was a kind of axis, a metropolis called central Canada, and a hinterland in the prairie provinces. We developed a national policy on transportation in such a way that there was resource extraction from the west, much of which for a long period of time was in the form of wheat. At the same time we saw the development of manufacturing at the centre, the metropolis. This policy was developed to some extent at the expense of the west. As this developed, and as tariffs were given to the east to protect the manufacturing industry-
And taken away.

-we found in the process that we were paying more in the west. The one concession that we in the west had was that we could depend on a statutory and stable rate for the movement of grain. But we now have a minister- who, I thought, having been involved in this commission, would understand the regions the best-working to the detriment of the prairie provinces.
He undermines his own report.

As the hon. member says, he is undermining his own report. We in the west, especially in Manitoba, have a particular problem with these proposals because Manitobans do not really stand to benefit from the development of the Rogers Pass and other things because most of our grain is shipped through Thunder Bay and through Churchill.
Not enough of it.

As the hon. member says, not enough of it. More should be shipped through Churchill.
I would now like to look at the Manitoba scene, especially the Tyrchniewicz Report of March, 1980. We should take a look at this report to see what the negative economic impact would be on Manitoba. This study was not done under a New Democratic Party administration in Manitoba; it was done under a Conservative administration. The Conservatives did not reveal the results of this study because, of course, they were afraid that their position might be untenable. Any educated person who looks at the report could see what the negative impacts would be on the Manitoba farmers if we had a removal of the Crow rate.
This study was done for the Government of Manitoba by three faculty members of the Department of Agricultural Economics at the University of Manitoba. One of their principle conclusions was that if the Crow rate were removed, on the hypothesis that the increase in freight rates would be 3.4 times the present amount times Crow, there would be a $50 million drop in farm output in Manitoba. It would cut the net farm income by an average $1,056 per farm. An area such as mine, the Parkland region, could not take such a loss. It is an undeveloped region and it is economically deprived. Many people do not have a net income of $7,000, never mind some of the higher incomes of people in urban centres. Many people live at the poverty level. In my constituency alone, there are seven Indian reserves with an average unemployment rate of 80 per cent to 85 per cent. Such a change would mean a terrible loss in these kinds of areas. This can be seen if one adds all the other increased costs of moving grain, let us say, by trucks, and the increased cost on roads. We would face a terrible loss in Manitoba. It is a real laugh to hear all the statements suggesting that a change in the Crow rate bring benefits to Manitoba.
Manitoba does not get a nickel.

In no way will we will see increased opportunities for the processing industries in Manitoba and other provinces because there are tariff barriers and restrictions which will not allow for the easy growth of these industries. In no way will eastern provinces support programs for their own industries when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is promising that the easterners will not suffer anything as a result of the change in Crow. There will be no opportunity for further development of processing industries in the west.
March 25, 1982

The other fear I have is that if the Crow rate is removed, we can expect the death knell to sound in places like the Port of Churchill and other ports which might otherwise be developed.
As far as Manitoba is concerned, there is no way that the removal of the Crow rate would provide any kind of economic benefit. I was quite troubled this afternoon while listening to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
Propaganda.

He is the minister who supposedly represents western Canada. I was amazed at his lack of understanding of some of the problems that we face there. An article in the Winnipeg Free Press, dated March 13, 1982, quoted him as saying that the Crow is one of the icons of western ideology. He has a complete lack of understanding. Actually, the Liberal Party is one of the icons in the west. One can find there only a few old pictures of Liberals.
It's an endangered species.

There was a meeting which took place in Fort Garry which, I believe, was called a two-day think tank, but it produced nothing but tanked thinking, as far as I can gather from the impact that it had on the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is really detrimental to the west to have the Minister of Employment and Immigration as minister, because he does not seem to understand some of the historic problems that we have faced in the west. Perhaps he should read some of the speeches made by Senator Hazen Argue in the other place. Even as late as November 27, 1981, the senator said that it is unlikely that changing the Crow rate would do much to stimulate the livestock and the processing industries on the prairies. That was his candid assessment of what would happen on the prairies. I think we ought to take cognizance of what the senator said in the other place. In fact, he said:
I don't intend to let the wool be pulled over my eyes and I don't believe that farmers can afford to have it pulled over theirs, either.
He is just a sheep, anyway.

I think Senator Argue was correct in stating that. He is a cabinet minister. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated where cabinet ministers should go if they disagreed with government policy. Senator Argue said further that the report prepared by Transport Canada earlier this year concluded that the impact of freight rates on the location of livestock and processing industries is exaggerated. I wish that the other members of cabinet would take cognizance of what some of their own members have said. They should take note of some of the wisdom in their own wisdom bank, rather than in their think tank, in terms of a fair and equitable policy with regard to the movement of grain in the west.
Hear, hear!

Let us take a look at some of the specific reasons for arguing that the Crow rate should be retained. The
Supply
distance over which we must move grain in western Canada to get to port is much greater than in any other competing country. However, in terms of our balance of payments, our grain exports are quite sizeable. It is in our own national interest to ensure that our agricultural economy is properly supported. Other countries do that. The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) mentioned earlier what competing countries, such as Australia, Argentina and the United States, do in terms of export of their grain. Our situation in western Canada is regionally different. As the Minister of Transport stated in his former report, there are regional diversities. I wish he would recognize these regional diversities and see that they are taken care of.
We should take a look at the whole question of tariffs, at the benefits they have brought to central Canada and how much they have cost other regions of Canada. I said earlier that the manufacturing sector in central Canada was able to develop because of tariffs. There is no manufacturing sector in western Canada to speak of. As a result of these policies and tariffs which enabled the central Canadians to develop their industrial sector, the prairies, with 16 per cent of the population, have been able to develop only 8.1 per cent of the manufacturing jobs.
Shame!

In anyone's books, this is inequality. This is an illustration of what I mean when I say we should take into consideration some of these other aspects. Certainly, many reports have recommended the retention of the Crow. I simply want to underline the following statement of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall in 1975:
If once tempering with the statutory (Crow) rate is accepted on condoned or is an item on the bargaining table, all will be lost. For once the subject is on the bargaining table, it will be only a matter of time until it is lost step by step.
In other words, what he said is that the economic forces would inevitably shift the total cost of grain transportation to the farmers. That is not the problem that producers of other commodities face. The coal producer can pass on his transportation costs, and Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan recognizes this. The potash producers can pass on the costs, but the farmers are not able to pass on their costs. They have no control over the price they receive for their grain. The farmers have no control over their input costs, no control over the costs of fertilizer, no control over the costs of energy. Their economy is squeezed; it is a cost-price squeeze. Farmers are always being forced into this vice.
The one item that they have had throughout the years has been the statutory Crow rate. Now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) wants to destroy this and with it destroy the agricultural economy of western Canada.
Arguments have been made about this, such as that if you give the railways more money the railways will do a better job
Supply
in transportation, that is if you give up the Crow rate. Yet, when you take a look at the facts, you see that the railways have not been doing their job, they have not been living up to their standards. The removal of the Crow rate will not solve this problem.
How do you know?

Mr. Speaker, I have a quotation here from George McGovern, the former United States senator from South Dakota. Speaking of the situation there, he said "We have a line here in South Dakota so bad that a boxcar fell off the track the other day and the train was standing still." They have variable rates there. Is that the type of transportation system we are trying to model ourselves after?
They have commercial rates.

They have commercial rates, as the hon. member says. Changing the Crow rate will only add to the railway's profits, not to improve the transportation of the prairie wheat. We have to keep this in mind when we look at this whole subject.
Some arguments have been made about the increase in grain traffic and the way grain is clogging up the railways. It is said that because of this you have to have railway expansion. Yet if we take a look at some of the statistics, we find that by 1990 the grain that will be marketed out through the west will be only 14 per cent of the traffic. Coal and potash will be the greater commodities marketed there. So, if the percentage of the grain commodity being exported there is going to be reduced, why should we place all the burden of transportation on the backs of the farmers, who already have been hit by this government's policies in so many ways? It is important for us to make sure that we see that our agricultural economy remains healthy, that our agricultural economy continues to thrive and flourish, because that is the only way that we in Canada as an entire country can ensure that we do meet all of our food needs.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I remind the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, the farmers out west-
What does a bushel of wheat look like, have you any idea?

Perhaps I should start off, Mr. Speaker, by advising the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) that I am a farmer, too, from southwestern Ontario. We have produced corn, soybeans, wheat, barley, beef cattle, laying hens. I say that just to have it on the record. I worked on a farm all my life. As a matter of fact, during the years of World War II, I helped my father on many occasions to unload western barley out of the boxcars to take it back to our farm to
March 25, 1982
feed it to livestock, ultimately to assist in the war effort to feed our troops in England and the troops of our allies.
I am delighted to take part in this debate today on a topic of vital interest to many Canadians. It has been an issue of extreme importance for so many years. Like all pieces of legislation that are in constant use, this particular matter should be updated to keep abreast of the modern facilities required to fill the world markets and use fully the productive capabilities of western Canada.
We know the Canadian Constitution was passed today in the British House of Lords. The old British North America Act was amended many times over the years, as required. So, too, must the Crow rate be re-examined to ensure that the farmers of Canada have access to world markets.
I would like to point out that the agri-food strategy report, presented by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in September last, points out that we in Canada can increase our production by a tremendous volume. But what good is this increased production if we do not have an efficient transportation system capable of delivering that product to the port of export or to the Lakehead?
Looking back, it is interesting to note that in 1908 and 1909 the rate from central Saskatchewan to Thunder Bay was about 18 per cent of the price of a bushel of wheat. Then, as wheat prices increased, that rate dipped to about 5 per cent in 1920. The same cost of transportation climbed to about 40 per cent during the 1930s, when the world wheat prices bottomed out. At the present time the price has dropped to about 3 per cent or 4 per cent of the cost of a bushel of wheat.
Surely the time has come when we must ensure that we do have the modern and updated facilities for the increased traffic, to benefit not only the farmers but the total agricultural industry and all the allied services that have an effect on our total economy.
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, we in Canada compete against the farmers in the nation to the south of us, who have a great inland waterway extending into the heartland of the production areas. We have to compete against the unit trains with modern non-stop unloading at some of the Gulf ports. We must also ensure that we provide the incentives here in Canada to modernize the system in a way that will allow us to compete aginst our neighbours to the south of us.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At 6 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
March 25, 1982
When the House rose at six o'clock, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was pointing out that if we as Canadians are to compete against the farmers of the nation to the south of us who have a great inland waterway extending into the heartland of their crop production areas, or if we are to compete against the unit trains with non-stop unloading, then we must ensure that we provide incentives and the modernized systems that allow us in Canada to compete, particularly those people in the prairie provinces.
We are no longer just referring to huge volumes of grain moving on these lines. We are referring to huge volumes of coal, sulphur and other goods and products for export. If we expect to have the services that are required for competition with other goods, I respectfully suggest that an adjustment is required now. 1 refer to the fact that grain shipments account for about 20 per cent of the traffic to the coast at the present time.
The government's total contribution to grain transportation since 1970 has been $1.7 billion. We have spent over a billion dollars in branch line subsidies in the last decade. We purchased 8,000 hopper cars in 1973, and in 1980-81 we leased another 2,000 hopper cars at an annual cost of about $12 million.
In 1974 we shared half the cost to the railways of $44.8 million for rehabilitating 7,200 boxcars. From 1977 to 1984, we spent or committed $495 million to upgrading and rehabilitating dependent rail lines in the prairie network. Between 1968 and 1982 we spent $23 million for port improvements at Churchill, Manitoba.
We are committed to $30 million for site development for the grain terminal at Prince Rupert, British Columbia. Since 1971 we paid $184 million to subsidize the movement of export flour and grain to Atlantic ports, mostly from elevators in the Georgian Bay area. Certainly the Government of Canada is prepared to commit additional funding over the next several years to assist in the movement of grain.
As a member of this Thirty-second Parliament from the province of Ontario, there is one point I want to make abundantly clear. Many people from western Canada feel that the Crow rate is of tremendous benefit to Ontario. This is no longer the case. In the last few years Ontario has been a net exporter of feed grains and is no longer a beneficiary of the rate. Other areas of eastern Canada do benefit to some extent, and also from the livestock feed freight subsidy that applies to eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
I hope we do not begrudge that assistance to those areas whose potential productivity or diversity of production is limited due to climatic and geographic locations and other conditions. It is also the areas that supplied scores of men from eastern Canada, not only Ontario but other provinces, who travelled west on the old harvest excursions to help with harvest there after the eastern harvest was completed. These were all forms of assistance that were provided to ensure that the harvest was completed in those days when there was not as
Supply
much competition from other goods moving on the rail lines. We were able to market the grain in a better form than we are today.
The question as to whether or not the Crow rate should be changed was not really an issue until the early 1960s. In 1961, the MacPherson Royal Commission on Transportation acknowledged an emerging railway revenue problem and recommended that subsidies be paid to the railway for losses incurred by reason of continuing utilization of light density lines and the Crow rate. As well, in the 1960s, the branch line rationalization process got under way.
The railways could neither maintain nor reinvest in the large branch line network, with the result that by the early 1970s the system began to deteriorate. In response to this situation, the federal government began to spend large sums of money, as I mentioned earlier, to purchase rolling stock and repair branch lines.
It was in 1975 that the then minister of transport, the Hon. Otto Lang, called for a change to the Crow rate by articulating his "bold approach" concept. The bold approach introduced the notion of Crow benefit which would result in a producer not having to pay the full cost of moving grain by rail in one increase. At that time his initiative faced severe opposition.
In 1975, the American consultant, Mr. Snavely, headed a one man commission to look into the cost of moving grain by rail. His report was released in 1976 and showed that the railways lost $103 million in 1974 for moving grain. His results were generally accepted by the west but no concensus as to who should pay the railways for lost revenue emerged at that time. In 1979, an updated report produced figures for 1977 losses of $160.5 million and a further update produced figures for 1980 which showed losses of $244.4 million.
In 1978, primarily because of transportation difficulties, the Canadian Wheat Board announced that it had to forgo or defer grain sales of approximately $1 billion. As a result, in January, 1979, the board ordered 2,000 hopper cars to be paid for out of producer funds at a cost of $87 million. At the same time, producers were forced to store grain on farms for longer periods and, certainly, interest rates were higher as well.
The result was a realization by many that the existence of the Crow rate was no longer in the producers' best interest. During the fall of 1979 the Crow rate became the major topic of discussion at many of the farm meetings.
Eventually, these discussions emerged mainly between two umbrella organizations; the Western Agricultural Conference and the Prairie Farm Commodity Coalition. These two groups each put forth a position requesting the federal government to address its responsibilities in the area of rail transportation.
Simultaneously, the matter of capacity constraints to the rail system through the mountains placed additional emphasis on the necessity of the railways to earn more money for

March 25, 1982
Supply
moving a commodity which represents 20 per cent of the railways' workload but provides only 3.5 per cent of the revenues.
Obviously, something had to change. One year ago, I was pleased to be invited to a meeting here in Ottawa which was called by some of Canada's farm leaders to hear their presentations on this issue. Their opinion was that by talking with each other and with us, as members, as well as with those directly affected, a workable solution could be found. I commend the minister for the action that he has taken in this response and I will be waiting for the recommendations from Professor Gilson which I believe will lay the foundation to enable us to update and modernize a system which will be a credit to this nation.
One point that I cannot agree with, however, is a suggestion by the NDP that we nationalize the CPR. I cannot accept such a far-fetched proposal because when I look at the CPR in my particular area-in fact, the Montreal to Windsor corridor-I find that the lines run parallel in most places and throughout most of that area, while the CNR lines are double tracked. This is a heavily travelled area for both rail lines. Is the NDP suggesting that we close one of these lines which are so heavily used and create a bottleneck which would be as critical to that area as that which we are trying to eliminate through the Rockies in the next few years? Are they suggesting that we nationalize a huge company which provides the only competition to our nationally run railway? Are they suggesting a move which would not improve the service but would most certainly place many people out of work? I strongly disagree with them.
I do agree, however, that the time has come, by any measure of comparison, to re-evaluate a program that has served us reasonably well for the last 85 years. But due to changing times and values, a broader scope of users and a need to compete in world markets, we simply cannot stand still. The Crow rate has served this nation well in the past but if we are to let our system rest on its laurels, we will end up with a system that has rusted on its laurels. Neither the prairie farmers nor Canadians will benefit.
The Government of Canada is taking these initiatives in dealing with the capacity problem in the interest of all Canadians. The whole economy will benefit from the opportunities which will be fulfilled as a result of these initiatives. The people of the three prairie provinces in particular will benefit because they have the capacity to feed a hungry world. They will be supplying those markets. However, as Canadians, we must ensure that the transportation system is capable of handling the volumes of grain and food which is produced to feed those hungry nations. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to speak tonight on this motion. I would like to congratulate the members of the New Democratic Party for introducing this motion. I think that it is most opportune and that the discussion at this stage is very proper.
I find the process set out by the hon. minister is good and I would like to review it for a moment. I like the proposal, that is provided it works out in the way in which I believe it can. Since I am not a prophet I am not saying that it will, but it is
capable of working to the advantage of Canada and western farmers-Canadian farmers for that matter.
The process as set out by the minister in a report from a Ministry of Transport release simply says that the consulation process will lead to a new statutory framework. I think that is axiomatic. If the Crow rate is to be replaced, I say that it certainly has to be replaced with something equally beneficial for those whom it now serves. It should be made statutory not simply a measure which can be changed at will or at the whim of any president of the CPR, or even at the whim of any government, without careful consultation.
The process involves $3.2 billion over the next four years- not $3.2 billion per year, but $3.2 billion over the next four years. This is assumed to be the shortfall between the Crow and the actual cost.
The next step in the process makes the assumption that the money will be paid to the railways. I am sorry to see that because I think that all avenues should be considered in deciding how this will be handled. However the proposal says that the railways will guarantee performance and service related to grain transportation in return for an improved level of financial compensation. I will deal with that point in a few minutes.
The railways will begin extensive investment programs and implement rate adjustments to encourage agricultural processing in western Canada. There will be intensive consultations with the affected parties in the west, which will be completed sometime this spring. Then during the summer, I understand the governments of the four western provinces will have an opportunity to consider those recommendations and to make representations of their own to the federal government and to the people. Finally, the matter will be brought to Parliament in the fall of this year.
It appears the process could work to advantage. There are one or two things I do not like too much about it. I do not like closed-door consultations. I think it would have been far better to admit the press as well as members of various organizations which are interested. However, I have faith in our agricultural leaders, and possibly this will work out. If secrecy is required after representatives of the various grain organizations leave the consultation table, I do not think that would be right at all. These people should have the right to come back and talk to their people and make further representations if that is necessary.
We are putting great faith in the railways, and the CPR in particular. I want to review briefly some of the things which have happened in the past and examine whether there is reason for putting such tremendous faith in the railways carrying out their obligations, whether they are set out in statute or otherwise. Let us go back to the beginning of the railways and when the CPR was offered $25 million and 25 million acres of land, including all its mineral resources, to build a railway across
March 25, 1982

this country. Twenty-five million dollars of about 100 years ago would have a value today of close to $1 billion when we take into account inflation and so forth. The railway received a very large sum of money. In addition to that large sum of money the railway received 25 million acres of land plus all its minerals. That was quite a gift. I do not think we can forget that today, because for that money the CPR promised to build a railway. This is what the agreement says: "perpetual and efficient operation of a railway." That means forever. How has that worked out? The CPR has reneged on passenger service. It ignored passengers for a very long time and finally got rid of them altogether. The CPR treated passengers very shabbily for a number of years and did not want to provide passenger service at all, but it was under an obligation under its agreement to carry passengers. The railway was paid for carrying passengers and, in my view, the Government of Canada had no right to let the CPR out from under that obligation simply by saying, "All right, we will forget about it." The railroad received millions and millions of dollars through mineral resources, and in return it was to operate an efficient railway perpetually. Now the railway has cast off half of that service. I do not think the people can forget that, and I do not think the government should forget it either. Governments have been guilty of not making sure the CPR lived up to that arrangement.
In about 1897 or 1898 the CPR was anxious to secure the rich coalfields of British Columbia. Again it presented a proposition to the government, and that led to the Crow rate. I want to read from the actual bill which was assented to on June 29, 1897. I will not read the whole bill. Although the whole bill is worth reading, I will read just two of its clauses. They read as follows:
Subject to the conditions hereinafter mentioned, the governor in council may grant to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company a subsidy toward the construction of a railway from Lethbridge, in the district of Alberta, through the Crow's Nest Pass to Nelson, in the province of British Columbia (which railway is hereinafter called "the Crow's Nest Line") to the extent of eleven thousand dollars per mile thereof, and not exceeding in the whole the sum of three million six hundred and thirty thousand dollars-
There was another three and a half million dollars paid to the railway to permit it to go into the rich coalfields of British Columbia. For that what did the railway promise to do? It said:
That the company will construct or cause to be constructed, the said railway upon such route and according to such descriptions and specifications and within such time or times as are provided for in the said agreement-
And it did.
It doesn't say with subsidies.

The bill went on to deal with the particular rates that were to be charged. Here is what the railway promised the rate would be: a special rail freight rate was to be applied to the transportation of export grains and flour from
Supply
shipping points in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba to Thunder Bay, Churchill and ports in British Columbia. The Canadian Pacific Railway entered into the Crow's Nest Pass Agreement with the federal agreement in 1897. As part of the agreement, the CPR agreed to maintain the Crow rate in perpetuity. Does that not mean forever? It did not mean just until 1982. It said forever, in perpetuity. The CPR received $3.6 million plus a number of other benefits in return for its promise to build a line into the rich coalfields of British Columbia. When I was a boy I used to wonder why everyone would laugh around the coalmines and say of the government, "Well, that is the CPR, isn't it?" They thought the CPR was the Government of Canada. I am beginning to think that too. The CPR apparently tells the government what to do, not the other way around.
It always has.

The CPR got out of passenger service after it was paid for getting into it. Now it wants to gets out of the Crowsnest Pass rate which it promised to keep in operation forever. I think that is something of which we should be mindful when we start looking at the proposition today.
I want to deal for a moment with the actual condition of the CPR. Perhaps it is poor. Perhaps it has had tough luck. Perhaps it has been beaten by inflation.
No, no.
Perhaps it will go on welfare. If it applied, I think it would probably get welfare from the federal government.
It is about time it went off welfare.

Let us look at the CPR's record. I have here its 1980 record. The CPR got its starts, as I said, with a gift of $25 million and 25 million acres of land, including mineral rights. In addition, it got another $3.6 million to build the line from Lethbridge to the mineral-rich Kootenay Valley in southern British Columbia. From this start it has expanded into a giant corporation, with current assets in 1980 amounting to $4,362 billion. That is only part of it. The company has properties valued at cost totalling $8 billion plus an investment portfolio exceeding $379 million.
That must be a sin.
It has other assets worth over $289 million.
Shame.

According to CP's actual 1980 report on its current accounts, it is making profits on almost everything. It is down a little with respect to truck transportation and one other enterprise, but on everything else profits are way up. The total profit for the year was very good-so much so that the company was able to provide a dividend of $3.89, I believe to the millions of people who invested in it. The only branch that earned less in 1980 than in 1979 was CP Telecommunications

and perhaps CP Air. CP Air is going through a bad period and could not be expected to provide much, but it still came up with $2.8 billion. In 1980 the only ones to lose money were CP trucks, CP Rail, CP Telecommunications, CP Air, CP Ships Navigation, miscellaneous hotels, and what have you. Every branch made a profit in 1980 except for CP trucks. They apparently know how to run a railway but they do not know how to run a truck line. They would have been wiser to stay out of the trucking business. They tried to eliminate the competition, but the truckers were too smart. CP is not a poor corporation; it has done exceptionally well. I do not say that it should have lost money. I am a free enterpriser and I like to see people make money. But I also like to see people live up to their agreements and not make their whole purpose in life the pursuit of money.
CP Rail could very well continue operating with the freight rate it agreed to guarantee forever. The profit record shows that it could still operate this way and come out ahead. I think the government has to be very careful about letting the corporation renege again on one of its obligations that it undertook for perpetuity.
I want to deal with some other points now, Mr. Speaker. There is a suggestion, which apparently arises from the annual report, and some farm organizations agree with it, that the shortfall of $3.8 billion should be paid to the railways. I have some misgivings about that. The railways have a pretty bad record of living up to their obligations. If we let them renege on their obligations, as we have done to date, it will be a poor deal and the western farmer in particular will be affected.
In his statement the minister said that there would be a guarantee, but what kind of guarantee, Mr. Speaker? Will it be a guarantee that the railways will not haul coal or sulphur or other minerals and let the wheat wait? I live in a coalmining area and I have seen carload after carload of coal and minerals go by while the wheat already loaded in the cars is not picked up. What kind of guarantee is there that the railways will haul the grain and give the farmers the service that they need?
Agriculture is a big industry in this country, Mr. Speaker. The farmers who raise barley and oats are important; they feed the world. I remember one time being at a meeting where a lawyer got up and said, "I plead for all". Then a minister got up and said, "I pray for all". A farmer got up and he said, "I pay for all." There is a lot of truth in that, Mr. Speaker. The farmer may be a livestock farmer, a beef farmer, a hog farmer, a horse farmer, a barley farmer, a potato or fruit farmer- there are all kinds of agricultural products.
I think the minister and the government should take a long look at agriculture when they are reviewing this plan. It is important that every phase of agriculture receive service. The minister spoke of getting a guarantee from the railway. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has referred to an ironclad guarantee. Well, this guarantee should be double ironclad. Like hundreds of farmers in the west, I do
not have faith in the CPR. It has not been fair to the western farmer and it has not lived up to its obligations. Simply paying over the shortfall to the company will not guarantee anything.
Perhaps we should examine the possibility of making the payment to farmers. A payment on an acreage or some other basis would have some merit and should be considered. The farmer could sell his grain wherever he wanted. He could haul it in his truck. He could feed it to his hogs or to his cows. He could send it by truck and compete with the railways. That would make the railways cut the lard out of their operations, if there is any. It would rationalize the whole thing. A lot of things could be done.
Order, please. I regret that I have to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I regret it too.

Mr. Speaker, I almost regret that the time of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has expired because I always enjoy listening to him. He has such a colourful way of putting across his views. I should like to make some comment about the approach he has taken to this issue, and, more important, about the approach taken by the member of the New Democratic Party who set down the motion.
What is at issue is whether we are going to make the hard decisions that are necessary in order to ensure that we have a rail transportation system in this country for the 1980s, the 1990s, the year 2000 and beyond that will provide the service required by western Canadian producers, to move their products from the point of production to the point of export or consumption. Are we going to worry about the future of this country, or are we going to continually squabble about the past? I for one opt for the future of this country and not the past, as does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
A similar and related issue is whether we are going to deal with Canadian problems in a way that will maximize our opportunities, or are we going to squabble amongst ourselves about trying to preserve the status quo? The status quo in western Canada is simply not good enough. There is great potential in western Canada and we must maximize the opportunities there and not squabble about how to preserve the present. Canada has always been a land of opportunity and we must maximize that opportunity.
Those are the issues involved in the Crow rate, the VIA Rail argument and so many other aspects of the discussions that we have had in the House over the last few months. I refer to the issues related to the budget, about whether we are going to get inflation under control or let it get out of control, about whether we are going to take the hard decisions that are necessary if we are going to have a prosperous future. Are we going to do these things or continue squabbling about things past until we find ourselves in a position where we cannot take advantage of the opportunities that we have and cannot
March 25, 1982

compete with the rest of the world? There is no reason whatsoever why Canadians cannot be at the top of the pile rather than half way down it.
Let us look at the Crow rate. What was it originally designed to do? Was it originally designed to be a subsidy? I suggest that it was not meant to be a subsidy. It was meant to be a stabilizing factor, so that farmers could count on a stable rate for the transportation of their product to markets across time. They could count on the rate because it would not fluctuate wildly. Were farmers from 1897 to 1925 to 1940 receiving subsidies from the railroads or from taxpayers? The answer to that is no, they were not. During the period from 1897 to 1925, the rates for handling grain were in fact somewhat below the statutory Crow rate. Farmers paid the full shot for moving grain. This was the same from 1925 and through the 1930s when costs and prices declined dramatically. Farmers were not receiving a subsidy from anyone, and they did not ask for a subsidy from anyone. They were paying the full shot up to 1940. In 1950 the situation was the same. Farmers paid the full shot of moving grain, and they were not asking for a subsidy or a handout.
In 1940 wheat was selling for $28 per metric ton. If we look at the cost of moving grain at that time, which was $4.28 per tonne, the relationship was approximately 17 per cent-the cost to farmers of moving their grain was about 17 per cent of the price of the tonne of grain which was being moved. In 1950, because of the inflationary period during the Second World War and shortly thereafter, the cost as a result of the statutory Crow dropped to 7.2 per cent. From 1950 to 1970 the relationship held constant; the relationship between the price of grain and the statutory Crow stayed at about 7.2 per cent. The cost to farmers relative to the price they were receiving for wheat stayed at about 7 per cent, which was down from 17 per cent during an earlier time. In 1980, when economic conditions changed dramatically in all western countries, the percentage of the cost of moving grain dropped from 7.2 per cent to 2.2 per cent. In the period from 1940 to 1980, the percentage of the total grain price, which in 1980 was $219 per tonne as opposed to $28 per tonne in 1940, dropped from 17.2 per cent to 2.2 per cent. Especially during the period from 1970 to 1980, a very real subsidy was obtained, whether it was a subsidy from the railroads or from Canadian taxpayers, as a result of the purchase of grain hopper cars and other infrastructure, branch line subsidies or whatever.
If we look at the problem of subsidies, we Find that, in the absence of remedial action, it is forecast at present the cost to farmers of transporting grain under the statutory rate, which was 20 per cent of actual cost in previous years, will fall to 12 per cent in 1985 and 7 per cent in 1990. I think that is important and relevant.
I have heard the arguments of hon. members opposite, which I think are false, that one reason for the Crow rate was to offset eastern tariffs which protected eastern manufacturers, that the protective tariff was absorbed by western farmers or westerners generally, even by people in British Columbia, and

that if eastern manufacturing was to be subsidized by Canadians, then western agriculture should be equally subsidized. Times are changing. We have now entered into a general agreement on tariffs and trade which will substantially reduce tariffs from 1981 to 1985; indeed on some products they will be gone altogether. Is it a valid argument that the justification for the Crow is the existence of tariffs to protect eastern manufacturers? If protective eastern manufacturer tariffs are being eliminated, should there not be an adjustment to the Crow?
I am not a lawyer, but when conditions change dramatically in the area of contract law, is it not true-and I am sure the lawyers in the House will correct me if I am wrong-that it can be raised as grounds for reopening the contract? If conditions change dramatically enough, such that one party is put at an extreme disadvantage with regard to another in a contract, is it not grounds for reconsidering the contract? In some cases I understand that it has been the case.
I would suggest that conditions have changed dramatically. What has changed dramatically? We went from very low rates of inflation and very low increases in the costs of doing business during the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s, to very high rates of inflation during the 1970s, which raised the cost to farmers of moving grain and in all other areas, such as the costs of fuel, seed grain, heating and labour. The costs of all these items rose, but the cost of rail transportation did not. If companies are expected to provide reliable transportation to move products to market, it seems only fair that they should be allowed to earn a fair rate of return, as the hon. member for Bow River indicated earlier. He believed that a fair rate of return should be available. He asked whether he could rely on CPR to move grain. What would happen, for example, if we in the House of Commons in our wisdom decided to tell Ottawa taxi-drivers that for some reason they had to transport Members of Parliament from the House of Commons to their residences at a rate which was only 20 per cent of the cost they could charge anyone else in Ottawa? How long would Mr. Speaker wait if he called for a taxicab from the House of Commons and said that it was for a Member of Parliament?
What would happen if they were given half of Ottawa?

It would be an extremely long time, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Bow River was concerned about moving grain, and I am concerned about moving grain. I want to see western agriculture and manufacturing being given the greatest possible opportunity. If the railways are able to obtain full tariff for moving potash, coal or other products, if the rail transportation system is already overloaded or running close to capacity and they had a free choice, what kinds of products would they move? They would move the ones on which they get full tariff, and in the case of taxi drivers, they would take passengers other than Members of Parliament.
