The grain is going to sit on the siding, and that is not acceptable. We have to find a way to ensure there is an economic benefit to the transporters to move that grain, and clearly right now there is none. The railroads lose money year after year moving grain when they can be making money moving something else. That is a not a situation difficult to understand for anyone who thinks about economic problems. If we do not allow a fair rate of return on every aspect of a company's business, it will take those areas where it does not make money and shove them aside. Western grain farmers are going to become second-class citizens, and we cannot allow that because we have a great potential in the grain growing regions of western Canada. The grain has to be moved.
In the last two or three years, Mr. Speaker, I have heard it said that because we could not guarantee the movement of grain we have lost as much as $1 billion to SI.5 billion worth of foreign sales.
If the railways had not been on strike.
Whether it be potash from Saskatchewan government mills, which is competing with grain growers in Saskatchewan and paying the full tariff, by the way-
I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.

The hon. member can ask his question at the end of my remarks. There is another point I would like to make, Mr. Speaker. As the hon. member for Bow River said, it is important that those who come to an agreement live up to the agreement; there is more than just money involved, there is honour involved, the obligation to live up to an agreement. I ask all members to consider the following. Last September an agreement was reached between two parties, the Government of Canada and the Government of Alberta. One of those parties is now saying that the agreement is no longer valid. I am not saying it is wrong, but why are they saying that? They are saying it because economic conditions have changed dramatically; the world price of oil has dropped. So, after nine months one party to the agreement says it is no longer valid, we have to renegotiate. And they are taking unilateral steps to force the other party to renegotiate.
I am not condemning that, Mr. Speaker. There might be good and valid reasons for it. However, I am saying that we have one nine-month-old agreement on which it is all right to renegotiate, but we have another agreement which is 84 years old which it is not all right to renegotiate. If economic conditions change, then certainly we are big enough in this country to open our eyes and see the consequences involved if we do not look realistically at the problem and renegotiate agreements which are totally and hopelessly out of date and out of touch with reality.
Were we to stay with the Crow rate as it is now, Mr. Speaker-the total transportation system is going to cover its costs, no two ways about that-what is going to happen is that
because grain farmers are not paying the full cost of moving their grain, the loss the railroads incur is going to be passed on to someone else. That will be the people who move potash, coal and other products. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it fair to ask the people moving those other products to absorb that additional cost which in turn may make them uncompetitive in world markets, and which may cost the jobs of people who work in the potash mines, coal fields and in the production of agricultural products not covered by the Crow? Is it fair to Canadian taxpayers generally to ask them to pick up part of that cost? These are questions which have to be asked, and the Minister of Transport has asked the questions.
When I was at the University of British Columbia my colleagues in the transport centre there were telling me the Crow rate has to be examined. No transport minister has had the courage to stand up and take that bull by the horns except for this one, and I applaud him for it. I think the process he has established is a fair one, and we will come up with a fair resolution of this problem. We will have the basis for developing an efficient and effective transportation system to increase and enhance the prosperity which is there to be had in western Canada.
I regret to advise the House that the hon. member, having used up all of his allotted time, can only be asked a question with the unanimous consent of the House.
No.
There is not unanimous consent. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) said the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) should be applauded for his actions. I think he is probably the only person doing so because if the minister were to come to western Canada today I am sure he could not beat A1 Capone in an election. That is about how popular the minister is, Mr. Speaker. It strikes me as rather curious to hear four or five Ontario members such as the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for London-Middle-sex (Mr. Bloomfield) and the member who has just spoken, get up and tell us how they are going to solve all the problems in western Canada. If the Liberal Party is so wise or, as the member says, the best in the west, why are there only two Liberals remaining in western Canada? I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if my constituents are any indication, those two members will not be here come 1983 or 1984.
Hear, hear!

As my friend says, it could not happen to a nicer guy if it happens to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
In addition, Mr. Speaker, it strikes me as rather odd hearing the hon. member for Ottawa Centre speak about the west as if we were back in the caveman's age and hauling our grain to
March 25, 1982

market on this rickety old transportation system which has not changed since 1897 or 1891. That is the impression he tries to leave with the House, that we have not modernized, we have not improved the branchlines or kept up the main line. I am not sure if he is aware, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of western Canada, the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Government of Canada have supplied some 14,000 hopper cars to move western Canadian grain. We indeed have modernized the system on the prairies. The Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan, for example, has 1,400 cars moving potash out of our province right now. The reason they have done this is that the railways went on strike many, many years ago in regard to moving grain from the prairies. The last time the CNR bought a boxcar to move grain was about 1947. For the CPR it was way back in 1951. Despite these facts, Mr. Speaker, we have a government across the way which stands up and defends the railways. We heard an excellent speech in the House tonight from the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). He spoke about the CPR, concerning all the money it had received, and the promises and agreements it had made to move the farmers' grain forever at a rate known as the Crow rate in this country.
I think, because of the speeches that I have heard here today and the incredible ignorance one sees exhibited on the government side of the House, that it might be very useful to spend a few minutes going over the Crow rate and presenting to the House, in a very positive way, what my constituents are saying to me and what the feelings of western Canadians are. I do this because the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis) rose in the House this afternoon and admitted that what the government was doing was a very unpopular decision, to use his words. I also remember the Speech from the Throne in April of 1980, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said to the country that despite the fact that the government did not have any elected members from the three western provinces, it would listen to western MPs in the House of Commons. I have gone through two years in this Parliament, and I wonder where the listening is evident, for the government is surely not hearing, if it is trying to listen. No matter where I go in my constituency, whether I speak to farmers or urban dwellers, people in my riding want the Crow rate kept. They see it as a part of the confederation bargain. They see it as a part of our nationhood. Ontario got the tariff protection. Ontario got freight rates which benefited the province. We got the Crow rate in the prairies.
Perhaps it might be useful to spend just a few minutes reviewing briefly the history of the Crow. Transportation has always been a part of national policy in this country, and it should be a part of public policy in Canada. If one looks back to 1881, at that time Canada needed a national railway to link central Canada with the west coast in British Columbia. A deal was struck with the railway companies, back in 1881. In return for building a railway to the west coast, the government gave the railways $25 million at that time, which would be
Supply
worth a lot more now, of course, because the value of the dollar has really diminished in the one hundred and some odd years. As well, the government gave the CPR 25 million acres of land with mineral rights. It gave the CPR many tax exemptions in addition. However, that was the deal and, in return for all the gifts and concessions, the railway was built to open this country and tie the west coast with central Canada.
Some 16 years later, in 1897, the federal government once again wanted to build a railroad. This time, it wanted to build a railway in the southeastern British Columbia end of the Crowsnest Pass. Therefore, once again, the government of the day said, "We will have to strike a deal. We will give you something if you will build a railway."
And they gave.

The government of the day decided to give the CPR 43.6 million and $3.7 million worth of land. In return, the CPR would do two things. First of all, it would build a railway into southeastern British Columbia. It would also guarantee that the rates on grain moving out of the prairies would be guaranteed for the settlers in the prairies of the day and that rates and settlers' effects moving from central Canada into the west would be regulated for the settlers who were opening up western Canada. That was the deal in 1897.
The hon. member for Bow River has spoken in detail concerning benefits granted to the CPR. One can now look at the CPR and see how it has benefited from this massive deal over the years. The CPR is probably the biggest welfare bum that we have in this country.
Hear, hear!

If we had done the wise thing over the years, which any investment person or businessman would have done, we would have taken equity in that railway and the CPR would have become a public utility many years ago and could served the Canadian people.
I would like to continue the history of the Crow, and I hope the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) will listen to this. During World War I, the agreement was suspended. By 1925 the CPR, to the surprise of no one, had persuaded the Liberal prime minister of the day, Mackenzie King, to get rid of the agreement, to cancel the agreement, to throw it out, because the CPR was saying, "We will lose money". That was way back in 1925.
Same old song.

But what happened in 1925 is something that I hope will happen today, 57 years later, in 1982. From the west, back in 1925, Members of Parliament representing farming and labour got up and debated, arguing to save the Crow. Because Mackenzie King needed political support in western Canada in order to maintain his government, he decided to relent, to call an agreement an agreement, and to save the Crow rate.
At that time, a couple of amendments were made which were very important. The first amendment was that the

Supply
railways could not tamper with the rates. In other words, there was a fixed rate for the movement of the farmers' grain on all lines moving the grain out to the ports. The other principle was that there should be equal rates for equal distance. In other words, a farmer in a little town in northern Saskatchewan, like Porcupine Plain in the riding of McKenzie, could ship grain to market for the same price as a person a couple of hundred miles south of the city of Weyburn because they were the same distance from the seaport. That was a very important principle. It meant that the railways could not set social policy by playing off one community against the other.
The other important result from the Crowsnest agreement back in 1925 was that the farmers were given a delivery system and elevators were built. An entire social and economic structure began to flower and flourish across the prairie provinces because there was a fixed rate for the movement of grain. There were no variable rates, so the railways could not play any games. A farmer could pick up the law books of Canada and he would know that he would be charged 18, 19 or 21 cents per bushel for the movement of his grain to the seaport.
What will result from the plan of the Liberal Party which sits across the way? First of all, the Crow will go. So said the Minister of Transport, when one has stripped away all the rhetoric, the flowery wording, the prose and the poetry in his announcement back in February. The minister will do three things. First of all, he will fix a rate for the railways in the statutes. He assures us that the railways of this country will receive guaranteed rates for moving the grain in this country. The railways instead of the farmers will have a statutory rate in Canada.
Shame, shame!

The second principle in the Liberal plan is that the producer should pay more. The farmer will pay more to move grain to market. The third principle in the Liberal plan is that there should be no fixed rate for the farmers of Canada. What will be missing, first of all, will be fixed rates under the Crow and, second, there will be no guarantee of equal charges for transporting grain equal distances.
What will be the consequences? The consequences will be very simple. In a few years' time, the effective rate for a farmer moving grain might be doubled or tripled. It will eventually go up maybe 10 or 20 times the present price a farmer pays to move his grain. This will mean that small farmers will be forced off the land. The minister may call that efficient. He may call it economy of scale. However, whatever he calls it, ordinary farmers in my riding will suffer. They will be pushed off the land because they will not be able to afford to farm.
The second consequence, when one considers variable rates, will be that the railway, the CPR, will determine social policy in this country because it will have the right to decide the rate from a certain town to a certain branch line compared to another town on a secondary main line, compared to a third town on a main line. If the rate will be, say, 10 cents or 20 cents a bushel higher on a branch line, farmers will obviously start hauling their grain to a secondary line or a main line, to a
different town, to a different community. Eventually, the elevator will close and the town will fold. The CPR will be making social and economic policy in this country. I say to Your Honour that that is not good enough and it is not right.
I want to mention two other points. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre went on at great length about the importance of being competitive and the importance of being efficient. I agree with him. It is very important that we be competitive and efficient, that we modernize the grain transportation system in western Canada. But I want to say to the member for Ottawa Centre that when we look at the Crow rate we must compare that in terms of a benefit to our farmers with what American farmers, Australian farmers and Argentinian farmers and European and other farmers are getting in other parts of the world. We are in tremendous competition with those countries.
If we look south of the border, for example, we find the Americans have subsidized the grain farmers massively-the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) knows this-in the program they have in the Missouri and Mississippi barge river systems. I think it was about $8 billion or $9 billion that was put into it by the government of the United States of America. They have done that, not only in the building of those systems but in their maintenance, to the tune of over half a billion dollars a year. Judge Emmett Hall said it was about $1 billion a year in terms of payments from the American government to maintain the transport system in the United States of America. From what I hear, in talking with senators and Congress members in the United States, it is not the intention of the American government to diminish those subsidies or to remove them. In other words, if we diminish what we pay in terms of an operating grant or a subsidy to our farmers in terms of the Crow rate and if the Americans do not, then we will be all that less competitive in the world scene, and we will probably sell less grain in the world.
Mr. Speaker, about five weeks ago I had a chance to go to Brussels and speak with the people in the European Common Market. I found that the Europeans give massive subsidies to their farmers. Once again, if they continue to subsidize their farmers and if we reduce the subsidy to our farmers, our farmers will be less productive and will probably sell less grain on the world market. That is important, that is important to all of us in this country, not just to farmers but to people in the cities-in Winnipeg, in Halifax, in Montreal, in Toronto or in Brantford or elsewhere-because the export of grain is a major benefit to all of us. In fact, in the first 11 months of 1981 our exports of grain were some $5 billion. That has a tremendous impact on the over-all wellbeing of all of us as Canadians. Lo and behold, we find the Government of Canada has not done any major studies whatsoever to assess the impact of reducing the Crow rate benefits to western Canada, on the over-all economy, or on the Canadian dollar, on the balance of payments, or on unemployment, or on any of these issues.

Mr. Speaker, if you look at it just from a competitive point of view, it is very important to all of Canada that we keep the Crow rate and keep it firm in law when other countries around the world give other subsidies to their grain producers. If you look at it from a bureaucratic point of view, the Crow rate system is probably the least costly and the most efficient way to help the grain farmer of any country in the world. We do not need hundreds of bureaucrats sending out cheques to farmers or assessing the income of farmers or assessing the income of the railways. All we need to do is to fix by statute the rate which we have had now for many years, and have that as our way of helping the grain farmers in western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, more and more people are becoming more and more concerned about the lack of real democracy. Once again we see the ugly head of hypocricy rearing itself in this Crow debate. We find a minister wanting to give to his cabinet, through order in council powers, the right to negotiate future increases in what the farmers will have to pay for the sale of grain. So in the future farmers will not have any direct input through their Members of Parliament from western Canada. Farmers will have to rely on the generosity of the sensibility of a federal government to set a reasonable rate for the shipment of this grain.
Mr. Speaker, that is like sending a skunk into the henhouse to collect your eggs. It is no wonder that more and more western Canadians are becoming alienated from the federal institutions that all of us in the House would like to keep, improve and democratize in the years that lie ahead. It is very dangerous that this government wants, once again, to take away from us our rights as Members of Parliament, representing our people, to get up and represent them in the House.
Thank God it is a statutory right and they cannot take it away, like VIA, without debate.

Mr. Speaker, that means that through the waving of a magic wand the Minister of Transport can decide to double the Crow rate, to triple the Crow rate, to put it up by ten times. Look at what they did with VIA Rail. They decided to get rid of all kinds of rail lines for passenger service. We did not have the right to have a committee look at it or study it. Members elected from western Canada did not have the right to get up in the House of Commons and vote-to vote on a bill to reduce the service to this country by VIA Rail.
I think that is dangerous, Mr. Speaker. It is giving awesome powers to government, awesome powers to bureaucrats and regulatory agencies, powers that are dangerous in a democratic society.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport was in Delisle very recently and got a little preview of the feelings on the prairies. If he is serious about holding this country together, perhaps he will change the bill that he is going to bring into this Parliament next fall and guarantee the Crow for western Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, the government has been talking about all the grants to railways. We have given hundreds of millions of

dollars to the CPR. We have the CNR, which is supposed to be a publicly owned people's railway. I suggest, in closing-

Mr. Speaker, in the eight minutes allotted to me I can say all that is necessary. First of all, I have heard the word "subsidy" in this so-called Crow debate too many times to sit silent. Let me say once again that there is no such thing as subsidy in the Crow rates. They are maximum rates. During most of the history of the railways in the whole of Canada, the freight rates paid by the farmers under the Crow agreement were the main profit source of the railways. For decades, 90 per cent of the profits came from the shipping of grain to foreign markets. We carried the people of Ontario and of southern Quebec; we carried the people of British Columbia on our backs, when they were losing money in those areas because of the competition of ships, or trucks that carried goods across the prairies, and when most had a losing operation by taking a profit out of the farmers.
I would prefer the word "subsidy" not used, because it is not a subsidy-and the record shows it.
In 1967, after ten years of intensive study by a royal commission, it was admitted to the House by the then minister of transport that there need be no more mention of the Crow in the House because we had proved for ten years that there were no losses on the Crow rates. These are the facts. No more should "subsidy" be talked about.
Mr. Speaker, a month ago I tried to steer this debate to what I thought was the crux of the situation. I think it has occurred several times today. Rightly or wrongly, the Crow rate in the minds of westerners is part of our Magna Carta, protecting our rights for what we did in opening up the west. No one is going to change that. It is just as sacred as is a constitution that lasts a thousand years. That does not mean it cannot be discussed; but do not try to push it across us that because the railways said they are losing money on the Crow we have to change a solemn agreement made long ago.
I am not going to go into any serious discussion about the Crow. Enough has been said. In my remarks a month ago I made very clear the minimum that would have to be done before there could be discussion. Before the minimum is done, it will be at least 20 years from now. Therefore, the discussion

March 25, 1982

led off by the minister's announcement a few months ago is really irrelevant.
What we are doing here today is curious. When the debate was led off by the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), I thought he was making an effort, which was unusual for him, to be constructive and to try to get people to sit down and discuss this rationally. All of a sudden the minister from Winnipeg, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) suddenly launched a direct frontal attack on the NDP.
I was watching the debate and wondered what was going on. The next speaker was from Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn). He smelled something irregular. When you find a minister of the Crown attacking the NDP, knowing how much they owe to the NDP for these last 15 years, you wonder. That member got up and told the story about two cats in Noah's Ark. Members know the story. It is as old as the hills. How are you going to keep the population down in a cramped little ark? Noah appointed a couple of giraffes to look into all the corners and make sure there was no funny business. When they ended the long trip and were going ashore, all the animals left the ark two by two. They were thanked for their consideration for each other. At the end of the row two cats came out.
We told that story earlier.

I am repeating the story to freshen your minds and to make clear what is going on here. When you have a situation where two cats appear to be fighting in the spring, common sense and experience tells you that they are not always fighting.
When the fight developed this afternoon, I thought it was funny that these two cats should be fighting. When I heard the story being told by the hon. member for Saskatoon West, I thought his intuition was right. It is spring.
All this talk today is only for one purpose. There is a Saskatchewan election in the offing. We wait minute by minute to see when it is going to be announced. It was obvious what the Liberals were doing. How could they help their allies in Saskatchewan? They could not help them by attacking the Conservatives. The only thing they could do was to crucify one of their loyal members. At one time he was the member for Assiniboia. He was the cat who tried to tell the farmers 15 years ago they had to believe in user-pay. He saw his boss, the former minister of transport, go down the drain. He went out and became the Liberal leader. He said he had changed his mind and was now for retention of the Crow. You can imagine Liberal cabinet ministers going out in public and crucifying this Liberal leader in Saskatchewan, saying he was not for retention of the Crow, he was a good loyal Liberal, and what Otto says he follows.
Otto, is he still around?

He is still around. He is vice-president of a grain company. I am saying that something funny is going on here. When you see two cats fighting, do not always believe what you see. We are simply
going through the preliminary ritual rhumba of an election in Saskatchewan. It is absolutely necessary that the Liberals appear to be opposed to the NDP. If they are not, how are the Liberals out there to know what to do? Now you see the situation, and I leave the answer to the public.
Why is this going on? It is simple to explain. There will be an election in Saskatchewan. What you hear and what you see ain't necessarily so.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very important debate we are having on this, an NDP opposition day. It is important for many reasons. After having listened to the debate, I find it unfortunate that there should be so much rhetoric and so little light shed on the problem. In many ways it is the responsibility of the government to shed light on this problem.
We all know there is a problem. The railways are not receiving enough money from the movement of grain to adequately compensate them and, as they tell us, ensure that they have enough capacity to move the raw materials that western Canada is capable of producing. Everyone realizes that, including the provinces.
The three prairie provinces have been involved. They have either bought or leased hopper cars. The federal government, to its credit, has recognized the problem. It has been involved in purchasing hopper cars and in a boxcar rehabilitation program. The producers have recognized the problem and, through the Canadian Wheat Board, have bought hopper cars to assist with capacity.
The lead speaker for the government was the minister from western Canada, the only elected member of the cabinet from western Canada, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I found it unfortunate that he did not set a little higher tone for the debate. He talked about enormous export increases for western Canada as a result of changing the Crow.
A lot of producers and members of this House would have been very interested to hear him tell us where these enormous increases will come from. He could have explained to us and the producers why a change in the Crow will have the effect of increasing exports. If it is going to increase exports, everyone would be in favour, but they would like to know why. We would also like to have been told that when we have the increased capacity to move grain and raw materials to export position, the government will be willing to follow through and look after Canadians in terms of the way we trade with other countries. We all know we had serious problems in the last series of GATT negotiations and how they ended up. It is true that many tariff barriers were lowered. For a period of eight years we are going to move to lower tariffs. We also know there are many non-tariff barriers which prevent Canadians from competing in markets such as the European Common Community and Japan.
If our government had seen fit to see that agriculture was better represented at those negotiations, it would be a lot easier
March 25, 1982

for producers and members from western Canada to have some faith and have trust in what the government is doing.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) pointed out that in many ways it is interesting that when we have this debate on a purely western issue the government does not really have any western members to stand up and talk about what it is intends to do in terms of western Canada. Today we heard from a parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) who was born in Saskatchewan but has lived in eastern Canada for a long time. A lot of western people watching this debate on TV and subsequently looking at Hansard will find it curious that that kind of member has to stand up on behalf of the government and tell us why in western Canada we have to do things differently.
In many ways I find it unfortunate that we should have the rancour, bickering and politicking going back and forth that we had today. That does not shed any light or give guidance to people genuinely concerned about the issue from a factual point of view.
That obligation does not end at the federal level. If we set a proper tone for the discussion and discussed it in terms of the issues and facts, it will be reflected back to the people we represent. On the same basis, the provincial governments have a responsibility. I find what the Premier of Saskatchewan said, as long ago as 1977, unfortunate. I will quote from an interview broadcast on CBC telelvision on Friday, May 20, 1977, close to five years ago. He said:
Because we believe that farmers are entitled to the Crow rate but we think that under certain circumstances, at some future time, the case might be made for increasing the level for Crow, provided that it was given the same statutory protection.
Clearly, as long as five years ago, the Premier of Saskatchewan was suggesting that there could be changes in the Crow. We all know that in the last four or five months he has continued to say that he is prepared to look at changing the level of the Crow. Yet when it comes time to review that, he takes an entirely opposite position.
I think it is unfortunate in many ways because, as I said, it does not shed a lot of light or provide much insight into the problem. It only confuses the issue.
This is a very serious matter for western Canada. It will have a profound effect on us for many years to come. I think it is the obligation of everyone, particularly the government since it is responsible for governing the country, to see that this decision is made with as much diligence as we can provide in Parliament.
I feel it is important to repeat that it is unfortunate today that we could not have had a discussion at a different level with respect to these problems and provided some solutions which would increase our productivity and our ability to contribute to Canada, instead of the politicking and rhetoric which we have witnessed.

I would like to close by simply saying that we all agree that there is a problem. I believe that it is up to us all to see that this problem is solved in a fashion which will benefit western Canadians with the best possible results. If this is achieved, it will result in a great benefit to all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to maintain the high degree of debate which the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) longs for.
This is chapter two in our series on western rail transportation and the Crow rate. I am sure that there will be many other chapters before we come to the end of this debate-
You can be sure of that.

-hopefully, by the fall, when we will be in a position to give westerners a much better statute for transportation of their grain than they have now.
At present, they have a statute which obliges them to pay only half a cent per ton mile but there is no equivalent obligation on the part of the railways to transport the grain. This is the root of the problem which we are faced with now. This is why the federal government had to take action in the recent past and buy hopper cars and proceed to branch line rehabilitation along with the other events which have taken place in recent years. I read recently that the Crow rate was dead from the moment the federal government had to begin buying hopper cars.
I think so.

During the debate on February 26 I tried to explain why we have to enhance the condition of the main line in the west and why we believe that the farmers will have to make a greater contribution to the transportation of their grain than they do now. I tried to answer the questions as to what guarantees the railways would have to give, which would be immensely greater than they give now.
Of course, I emphasized the great contribution that the federal government would be making through adding $1.3 billion to the $1.8 billion for four years already committed by it to grain transportation.
What has happened since our announcement on February 8 in Winnipeg? A moment ago, one of the members of the Conservative Party complained that they were not given much attention. The reason for that is quite obvious. We are sympathetic to their position because they are totally divided and, being charitable people, we do not want to exploit that situation. That is why we pick on our friends in the NDP, because at least they are offering a target which the Conservatives, unfortunately, are not.
I am just pointing out to the hon. member for Portage-Marquette that it is the NDP which have provided the opposition to us on this matter. It is not particularly the federal NDP either; opposition has come primarily from the Saskatchewan provincial NDP partly because of a certain election-as the

hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) indicated-which may take place in that particular province in the near future.
I have found what they have been saying to be rather interesting and I have been following what has been said in all the papers. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I am of the class of '63 in the House-I recognize I have been on holidays for nearly seven years-but for the past 20 years I have seen my party subjected to the daily moral reprimands of those political monks and nuns who form the New Democratic parliamentary wing. Well, I have news for you. They are not beyond temptation and they are not beyond sin. We have had an illustration of that today. They have a way of occasionally powdering figures and powdering concepts, which is really their trademark. We saw evidence of that today. They have found a way to distort the 1880 and 1897 agreements, the Canadian Pacific and Government of Canada railway construction agreement of 1880 and the Crowsnest agreement of 1897. I do not need to display my intellectual capacity because these distortions have been proven in many books and articles. There is a recent one on Sifton which corrects all the interpretations made by the member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), who looks like a Rhodes scholar and probably was one. What the NDP are repeating today are perceptions which have been found to be incorrect in history and which a number of authors have debunked.
Tell us about the shares in Power Corporation.

You see, that is a very intelligent argument. It has been used in Saskatchewan. Somebody said that it was because I served on the board of Power that I was supporting CP in this matter since Power has shares in CP. This is nasty, brutish, short and particularly immoral because when I was on the board of Power it did not have a share in CP. These are the kinds of arguments that are made by those saintly people over there who take pride in being superior to everyone else and in this particular instance, as in many, really lie. I find that remark particularly disagreeable and nasty.
Hear, hear!
Tell us about Ottawa Pioneer Grain. Tell us that has nothing to do with this.

We have heard again this afternoon certain interpretation of the meaning of the Hall Commission. Hall has suddently become a great expert on the Crow. When you read the book, you find he has hardly four or five pages on the subject, and some of it is contradictory. Nevertheless, this is the rewriting of history that the members from the NDP resort to. There is a quote which I will have to refer to next time, a feuilleton, which says that this government will introduce the variable rates in Saskatchewan. This is being repeated every day. The Prime Minister was in Saskatchewan recently and said that if western farmers do not want variable rates, there will be no variable rates. They keep repeating that, and I have it here. It reads:
The Pepin plan eliminates a fixed rate in law for the movement of grain and it eliminates equal rates for equal distance.
That is not true. I hope that it is parliamentary, when it is true, to say, and there is no other way to say it, that it is a lie.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Like double tracking.

That is true. It is being done now.
To continue with this statement, it said:
In doing so, it threatens the social and economic fabric of rural Saskatchewan.
So the introduction of the variable rates which most probably will not be introduced-
Oh, oh!
Most probably?

We have not done it. The point I want to make is that that concentration or consolidation is a phenomenon which has already taken place in Saskatchewan. Perhaps a few figures will illustrate that. The number of permits in the west has gone done from 200,000 to 140,000. The sizes of farms have grown. There has been a reduction in the number of country elevators from 5,200 in 1970 to 3,090 now. The number of delivery points has also been reduced, from 1,835 in 1970 to 1,245 now. There has been a reduction in the number of grain companies. That consolidation which hon. members opposite fear we might bring about already exists in the west. This is not something that the "dirty" Liberals or "nasty" Liberals or "immoral" Liberals are going to create. This is something which already exists. Why does it exist? It exists for a number of reasons. The economics of primary elevators is one of those reasons. As elevators have become obsolete in the west they have been replaced by bigger ones with better health standards, better working conditions and what not. Indeed, some smaller elevators have disappeared and a number of social entities have been downgraded because of their disappearance. That is a fact of life. This was not created by variable rates or a reduction of the Crow rate, which has not yet taken place.
I love to read at night, and I have been reading some material from Mr. Justice Hall. He said this:
Rural electrification has no doubt had the most significant positive social impact on rural life . . . Due to the ability to keep bread, fresh vegetables and fruits for a longer period, these commodities were purchased in greater quantity, farther from home leading to the closing of local bakeries and stores.
The phenomenon of consolidation has been studied by Mr. Justice Hall. I repeat, it did not take place today. It will not take place in the future. It has already taken place. It is due to a number of factors, some of them economic and some of them social. For example, some consolidation has taken place by virtue of action taken by the province of Saskatchewan. It is the Saskatchewan government which has presided over the concentration of schools and the elimination of schools where there were not enough students. It is the Government of Saskatchewan which has contributed to the concentration of

social services, hospital services and the like. I have all the figures here for those who would care to have them.
They don't care.

This consolidation has also been the will of the people of Saskatchewan. It was not imposed on them. This afternoon we were told we presided over the destruction of rural life in Saskatchewan-for something we have not done yet, by the way-because of something which took place when the Crow was still in existence. Hon. members opposite should think a little bit.
Impossible.

Hon. members should listen to what Mr. Justice Hall said on this particular point because it is beautiful. This concentration of rural life in Saskatchewan, as he said:
-took place, not as a part of a planned development-
Not because of nasty politicians.
Liberal politicians.

Listen to that scholar.
-but as a result of many people making individual decisions on where they wished to shop, do business and socialize.
It was because they wanted to do it.
It is the people and the spirit of the people which gives the community viability, not the railways nor the elevators.
Consolidation is a decision of the people in Saskatchewan. They made these decisions before there was any possibility of reducing the Crowsnest rate or of having variable rates. And again, that decision has not yet been taken. I cannot judge all the things members of the New Democratic Party do, but in this matter they are really misinforming the public when they say that increasing the Crow rate will destroy rural life in Saskatchewan.

He accused the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) of being a bad westerner.
Right on.
